subject.name: Physics
subject.description: Cambridge IGCSE Physics. Core students take Papers 1 and 3; Extended students take Papers 2 and 4. Momentum (1.6) is Extended content only. Calculations use g = 9.8 N/kg, and you can type answers in standard form, for example 3.0e8. The practical papers (5 and 6) are not included. The questions are original practice questions written in the style of Cambridge papers, not reproduced past paper material.

topics.title: Physical quantities and measurement techniques
topics.summary: Measuring length, volume and time; scalars and vectors.

topics.title: Motion
topics.summary: Speed, velocity, acceleration, distance–time and speed–time graphs.

topics.title: Mass and weight
topics.summary: Mass, weight and gravitational field strength.

topics.title: Density
topics.summary: Calculating and measuring density; floating and sinking.

topics.title: Forces
topics.summary: Effects of forces, turning effect, centre of gravity.

topics.title: Momentum
topics.summary: Momentum, impulse and conservation of momentum (Extended).

topics.title: Energy, work and power
topics.summary: Energy stores and transfers, work, power, energy resources.

topics.title: Pressure
topics.summary: Pressure on surfaces and in liquids.

topics.title: Kinetic particle model of matter
topics.summary: States of matter, particle model, gases and pressure.

topics.title: Thermal properties and temperature
topics.summary: Thermal expansion, specific heat capacity, melting, boiling and evaporation.

topics.title: Transfer of thermal energy
topics.summary: Conduction, convection and radiation.

topics.title: General properties of waves
topics.summary: Wave motion, transverse and longitudinal waves, reflection, refraction, diffraction.

topics.title: Light
topics.summary: Reflection, refraction, thin lenses, dispersion.

topics.title: Electromagnetic spectrum
topics.summary: Regions, uses and dangers of electromagnetic waves.

topics.title: Sound
topics.summary: Production, speed and reflection of sound; ultrasound.

topics.title: Simple phenomena of magnetism
topics.summary: Magnets, magnetic fields and materials.

topics.title: Electrical quantities
topics.summary: Charge, current, e.m.f., potential difference, resistance, energy and power.

topics.title: Electric circuits
topics.summary: Series and parallel circuits, potential dividers.

topics.title: Electrical safety
topics.summary: Hazards, fuses, circuit breakers and earthing.

topics.title: Electromagnetic effects
topics.summary: Induction, the a.c. generator, motors, transformers.

topics.title: The nuclear model of the atom
topics.summary: Atomic structure, nuclide notation, the nucleus.

topics.title: Radioactivity
topics.summary: Detection, types of emission, decay, half-life, safety.

topics.title: Earth and the Solar System
topics.summary: The Earth, the Moon, the Sun and planets, orbits.

topics.title: Stars and the Universe
topics.summary: The Sun as a star, stellar life cycles, the Universe and the Big Bang.

parts.prompt: Which quantity is a vector?

markingPoints.text: D – velocity

parts.examinerComment: Velocity has direction; speed does not.

parts.prompt: A car travels {=v*t} m in {t} s. What is its average speed?

markingPoints.text: B – {v} m/s

parts.examinerComment: speed = distance ÷ time.

parts.prompt: What is the weight of a {m} kg mass on Earth? (g = 9.8 N/kg)

markingPoints.text: D – {=round(m*9.8,3)} N

parts.examinerComment: W = mg.

parts.prompt: A block has a mass of {=rho*V} g and a volume of {V} cm³. What is its density?

markingPoints.text: B – {rho} g/cm³

parts.examinerComment: density = mass ÷ volume.

parts.prompt: A spring extends by {k} cm for each 1.0 N of load, within its limit of proportionality. What is its extension with a {F} N load?

markingPoints.text: D – {=k*F} cm

parts.examinerComment: The extension is proportional to the load.

parts.prompt: In which energy store is energy kept in a stretched spring?

markingPoints.text: B – elastic (strain)

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: A force of {=p*A} N acts on an area of {A} m². What is the pressure?

markingPoints.text: C – {p} Pa

parts.examinerComment: p = F ÷ A.

parts.prompt: What causes the pressure of a gas on the walls of its container?

markingPoints.text: A – particles colliding with the walls

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: Why are small gaps left between sections of railway track?

markingPoints.text: A – to allow for thermal expansion

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: Which process can transfer thermal energy through a vacuum?

markingPoints.text: D – radiation

parts.examinerComment: Conduction and convection need particles.

parts.prompt: A wave has a frequency of {f} Hz and a wavelength of {lam} m. What is its speed?

markingPoints.text: D – {=f*lam} m/s

parts.examinerComment: v = fλ.

parts.prompt: Light strikes a plane mirror with an angle of incidence of {i}°. What is the angle of reflection?
parts.examinerComment: Angles are measured from the normal.

parts.prompt: Which part of the electromagnetic spectrum has the longest wavelength?

markingPoints.text: B – radio waves

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: What is the approximate range of human hearing?

markingPoints.text: B – 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: Two magnets are placed with their north poles facing each other. What happens?

markingPoints.text: B – They repel.

parts.examinerComment: Like poles repel.

parts.prompt: How is an ammeter connected to measure the current through a lamp?

markingPoints.text: B – in series with the lamp

parts.examinerComment: Voltmeters are connected in parallel.

parts.prompt: A {R1} Ω resistor and a {R2} Ω resistor are connected in series. What is the combined resistance?
parts.examinerComment: Resistances in series add.

parts.prompt: What is the purpose of a fuse in a plug?

options.text: to melt and break the circuit if the current is too high

markingPoints.text: C – to melt and break the circuit if the current is too high

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: A magnet is pushed into a coil connected to a meter. Which change increases the induced e.m.f.?

markingPoints.text: A – moving the magnet faster

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: What does the nucleus of an atom contain?

markingPoints.text: C – protons and neutrons

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: Which type of radiation is the most strongly ionising?

markingPoints.text: A – alpha

parts.examinerComment: Alpha is the most ionising and the least penetrating.

parts.prompt: How long does the Earth take to orbit the Sun?

markingPoints.text: C – about 365 days

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: Which statement about the Sun is correct?

It is the largest star in the Universe.
It produces energy by burning coal.

markingPoints.text: B – It is a medium-sized star made mostly of hydrogen and helium.

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: What is the momentum of a {m} kg trolley moving at {v} m/s?

markingPoints.text: D – {=m*v} kg m/s

parts.examinerComment: p = mv. Squaring the speed gives kinetic energy, not momentum.

parts.prompt: A stack of {n} sheets of paper is {=round(n*s,2)} mm thick. Calculate the thickness of one sheet, in mm.

markingPoints.text: C1 for {=round(n*s,2)} ÷ {n}
A1 for {=round(round(n*s,2)/n,4)} mm

parts.examinerComment: Measuring many sheets and dividing reduces the uncertainty.

parts.prompt: A cyclist accelerates from rest to {v} m/s in {t} s. Calculate the acceleration, in m/s².

markingPoints.text: C1 for a = Δv ÷ t
A1 for {=round(v/t,3)} m/s²

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: State two differences between mass and weight.

markingPoints.text: mass is the quantity of matter; weight is a gravitational force
mass is measured in kg; weight in N
weight changes with gravitational field strength; mass does not

parts.examinerComment: Many candidates gave units only. Defining each quantity earns more credit.

parts.prompt: Describe how to find the density of an irregularly shaped stone.

markingPoints.text: measure the mass using a balance
find the volume by displacement: the rise in water level in a measuring cylinder
density = mass ÷ volume

parts.examinerComment: Answers should name the measuring instruments.

parts.prompt: A force of {F} N acts {d} m from a pivot, at right angles to the line from the pivot. Calculate its moment, in N m.

markingPoints.text: C1 for moment = force × perpendicular distance
A1 for {=round(F*d,3)} N m

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: A crate of weight {W} N is lifted through a height of {h} m. Calculate the work done, in J.

markingPoints.text: C1 for W = Fd
A1 for {=W*h} J

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: Explain why tractors used on soft ground have wide tyres.

markingPoints.text: wide tyres give a larger area
so the pressure on the ground is smaller and the tractor sinks less

parts.examinerComment: Answers must link area to pressure.

parts.prompt: Describe the motion of particles in a gas.

markingPoints.text: random motion
at high speed, in straight lines between collisions

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: Name the process in which a liquid changes to a gas at its surface, at a temperature below its boiling point.

markingPoints.text: evaporation

parts.examinerComment: Boiling happens throughout the liquid at its boiling point.

parts.prompt: Explain why a metal spoon in a cup of hot tea quickly feels hot.

markingPoints.text: thermal energy is transferred by conduction
metals are good conductors because they have free (delocalised) electrons

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: Define the wavelength of a wave.

markingPoints.text: the distance between two adjacent crests (or corresponding points)

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: State two characteristics of the image formed by a plane mirror.

markingPoints.text: virtual
same size as the object
upright
same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front
laterally inverted

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: Give one use of microwaves.

markingPoints.text: cooking / satellite communication / mobile phones

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: A student claps near a cliff and hears the echo {t} s later. The speed of sound is {v} m/s. Calculate the distance to the cliff, in m.

markingPoints.text: C1 for distance travelled = {v} × {t} = {=v*t} m
C1 for halving: the sound travels there and back
A1 for {=v*t/2} m

parts.examinerComment: Many forgot that the sound travels to the cliff and back.

parts.prompt: Name a magnetic material.

markingPoints.text: iron, nickel, cobalt or steel

parts.examinerComment: Aluminium and copper are not magnetic.

parts.prompt: The potential difference across a resistor is {Vv} V and the current is {I} A. Calculate its resistance, in Ω.

markingPoints.text: C1 for R = V ÷ I
A1 for {=round(Vv/I,2)} Ω

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: Two {R} Ω resistors are connected in series to a {Vb} V battery. Calculate the current, in A.

markingPoints.text: C1 for total resistance = {=2*R} Ω
A1 for {=round(Vb/(2*R),3)} A

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: Explain why the earth wire is connected to the metal case of an appliance.

markingPoints.text: if a live wire touches the case, current flows to earth
the large current melts the fuse, so the case does not stay live and the user is not electrocuted

parts.examinerComment: Good answers linked the earth wire to the fuse.

parts.prompt: State one way to increase the force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field.

markingPoints.text: increase the current / use a stronger magnet

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: A nuclide of uranium is ²³⁸₉₂U. How many neutrons does its nucleus contain?

markingPoints.text: B1 for 146

parts.examinerComment: Neutrons = nucleon number − proton number.

parts.prompt: A radioactive sample has a half-life of {T} hours. Its count rate is {=k*2^n} counts/minute. Calculate the count rate after {=n*T} hours, in counts/minute.

markingPoints.text: C1 for {n} half-lives
A1 for {k} counts/minute

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: Explain why the Earth has day and night.

markingPoints.text: the Earth rotates on its axis
once every 24 hours, so each side faces towards and then away from the Sun

parts.examinerComment: Some said the Earth orbits the Sun once a day.

parts.prompt: What does a light-year measure?

markingPoints.text: distance (the distance light travels in one year)

parts.examinerComment: It is not a unit of time.

questions.stem: Fig. 1 shows a series circuit.

figures.alt: Circuit diagram: a 12 V cell in series with a 4.0 Ω resistor, a 2.0 Ω resistor and an ammeter.
figures.caption: Fig. 1

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Calculate the reading on the ammeter, in A.

markingPoints.text: C1 for total resistance = 6.0 Ω
A1 for 2.0 A

parts.examinerComment: Resistances in series add.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Calculate the potential difference across the 4.0 Ω resistor, in V.

markingPoints.text: C1 for V = IR
A1 for 8.0 V

parts.examinerComment: The p.d.s across the resistors add up to the supply voltage.

questions.stem: Fig. 2 shows the speed–time graph for a cyclist.

figures.alt: Speed–time graph: speed rises steadily from 0 to 10 m/s in 4 s, stays at 10 m/s until 10 s, then falls to 0 at 12 s.
figures.caption: Fig. 2

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Describe the motion of the cyclist between 4 s and 10 s.

markingPoints.text: constant speed of 10 m/s

parts.examinerComment: 'Not moving' was a common misreading of a horizontal line.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Calculate the total distance travelled by the cyclist, in m.

markingPoints.text: C1 for area under the graph
A1 for 90 m

parts.examinerComment: Splitting the area into triangles and a rectangle helps.

questions.stem: Fig. 4 shows how the count rate from a radioactive source changes with time. The background count has been subtracted.

figures.alt: Graph of count rate against time: the count rate falls from 800 counts per minute at 0 hours, halving every 2 hours.
figures.caption: Fig. 4

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Use Fig. 4 to find the half-life of the source, in hours.

markingPoints.text: C1 for reading the time for 800 to fall to 400
A1 for 2.0 hours

parts.examinerComment: Draw lines on the graph to show your reading.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Find the count rate after 4.0 hours, in counts per minute.

markingPoints.text: B1 for 200

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: Forces of {F1} N east and {F2} N north act on an object. Calculate the magnitude of the resultant force, in N.

markingPoints.text: C1 for √({F1}² + {F2}²)
A1 for {=round(sqrt(F1^2+F2^2),2)} N

parts.examinerComment: Forces at right angles are added using Pythagoras' theorem, not by adding.

parts.prompt: A train accelerates uniformly from rest to {v} m/s in {t} s. Calculate the distance travelled in this time, in m.

markingPoints.text: C1 for area under the speed–time graph: ½ × {t} × {v}
A1 for {=0.5*v*t} m

parts.examinerComment: Multiplying final speed by time gives twice the correct answer.

parts.prompt: An astronaut has a mass of {m} kg. The gravitational field strength on the Moon is 1.6 N/kg. Calculate the astronaut's weight on the Moon, in N.

markingPoints.text: C1 for W = mg
A1 for {=1.6*m} N

parts.examinerComment: The astronaut's mass does not change.

parts.prompt: An object of density 0.90 g/cm³ is placed in water of density 1.0 g/cm³. State and explain whether it floats or sinks.

markingPoints.text: it floats
because its density is less than that of water

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: Calculate the resultant force needed to give a car of mass {m} kg an acceleration of {a} m/s², in N.

markingPoints.text: C1 for F = ma
A1 for {=m*a} N

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: A force of {F} N acts on a ball for {t} s. Calculate the impulse, in N s.

markingPoints.text: C1 for impulse = FΔt
A1 for {=round(F*t,3)} N s

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: A {m1} kg trolley moving at {v} m/s collides with a stationary {m2} kg trolley and they stick together. Calculate their speed after the collision, in m/s.

markingPoints.text: C1 for momentum before = {=m1*v} kg m/s
A1 for {=round(m1*v/(m1+m2),3)} m/s

parts.examinerComment: Momentum is conserved; kinetic energy is not.

parts.prompt: Calculate the kinetic energy of a {m} kg ball moving at {v} m/s, in J.

markingPoints.text: C1 for Eₖ = ½mv²
A1 for {=round(0.5*m*v^2,3)} J

parts.examinerComment: Squaring only the speed, not the product mv, was essential.

parts.prompt: Calculate the change in pressure at a depth of {h} m in water of density 1000 kg/m³, in Pa. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

markingPoints.text: C1 for Δp = ρgΔh
A1 for {=round(9800*h,1)} Pa

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: A fixed mass of gas at constant temperature has a pressure of {p1} kPa and a volume of {V1} m³. It is compressed to {V2} m³. Calculate the new pressure, in kPa.

markingPoints.text: C1 for p₁V₁ = p₂V₂
A1 for {=round(p1*V1/V2,2)} kPa

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: Calculate the energy needed to raise the temperature of {m} kg of water by {dT} °C, in J. (specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J/(kg °C))

markingPoints.text: C1 for ΔE = mcΔθ
A1 for {=4200*m*dT} J

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: Water in a pan is heated from below. Explain how a convection current forms.

markingPoints.text: water near the heat source expands
becomes less dense and rises
cooler, denser water sinks to take its place

parts.examinerComment: 'Heat rises' is not acceptable. It is the less dense water that rises.

parts.prompt: Water waves travel from deep water into shallow water. State what happens to their speed, wavelength and frequency.

markingPoints.text: speed decreases
wavelength decreases
frequency stays the same

parts.examinerComment: Frequency is set by the source and does not change.

parts.prompt: A ray of light passes from air into glass. The angle of incidence is {i}° and the angle of refraction is {=round(i*q)}°. Calculate the refractive index of the glass, to 3 significant figures.

markingPoints.text: C1 for n = sin i ÷ sin r
C1 for sin {i}° ÷ sin {=round(i*q)}°
A1 for {=round(sin(i*pi/180)/sin(round(i*q)*pi/180),3)}

parts.examinerComment: Calculators must be in degree mode.

parts.prompt: State the speed of electromagnetic waves in a vacuum, in m/s.

markingPoints.text: B1 for 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s

parts.examinerComment: Answers can be typed as 3.0e8 or 3.0 × 10^8.

parts.prompt: Explain why sound cannot travel through a vacuum.

markingPoints.text: sound needs a medium / particles
because it travels as vibrations of particles (a longitudinal wave)

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: Describe how to plot the magnetic field lines around a bar magnet using a plotting compass.

markingPoints.text: place the compass near one pole and mark the direction the needle points
move the compass so its tail is at the last mark and repeat
join the dots to form a line, from N to S, and repeat from other starting points

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: A current of {I} A flows for {t} minutes. Calculate the charge that passes, in C.

markingPoints.text: C1 for Q = It with t = {=t*60} s
A1 for {=round(I*t*60,2)} C

parts.examinerComment: Minutes must be converted to seconds.

parts.prompt: Calculate the combined resistance of a {R1} Ω resistor and a {R2} Ω resistor connected in parallel, in Ω.

markingPoints.text: A1 for {=round(R1*R2/(R1+R2),3)} Ω

parts.examinerComment: The combined resistance must be less than the smallest resistor.

parts.prompt: A kettle is rated at 2300 W, 230 V. Calculate the current and choose a suitable fuse from 3 A, 5 A and 13 A.

markingPoints.text: current = 2300 ÷ 230 = 10 A
13 A fuse (the next value above the normal current)

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: A transformer has {Np} turns on its primary coil and {Ns} turns on its secondary coil. The primary voltage is 230 V. Calculate the secondary voltage, in V.

markingPoints.text: C1 for Vₛ/Vₚ = Nₛ/Nₚ
A1 for {=round(230*Ns/Np,3)} V

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: Describe what the alpha-particle scattering experiment showed about the structure of the atom.

markingPoints.text: most alpha particles passed straight through, so the atom is mostly empty space
a few were deflected through large angles
so the nucleus is very small, dense and positively charged

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: Radium-226 (²²⁶₈₈Ra) decays by alpha emission to radon (Rn). Write the nuclide equation.

markingPoints.text: ²²⁶₈₈Ra → ²²²₈₆Rn + ⁴₂α
nucleon and proton numbers balance on both sides

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.prompt: The Earth orbits the Sun at an average radius of 1.5 × 10¹¹ m with a period of 3.2 × 10⁷ s. Calculate its average orbital speed, in m/s.

markingPoints.text: C1 for v = 2πr ÷ T
A1 for 2.9 × 10⁴ m/s

parts.examinerComment: Answers can be typed as 2.9e4.

parts.prompt: The Hubble constant is about 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹. Estimate the age of the Universe, in s, using 1 ÷ H₀.

markingPoints.text: A1 for 4.5 × 10¹⁷ s

parts.examinerComment: Answers can be typed as 4.5e17.

questions.stem: Fig. 2 shows the speed–time graph for a cyclist.

figures.alt: Speed–time graph: speed rises steadily from 0 to 10 m/s in 4 s, stays at 10 m/s until 10 s, then falls to 0 at 12 s.
figures.caption: Fig. 2

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Calculate the acceleration of the cyclist during the first 4 s, in m/s².

markingPoints.text: C1 for gradient = 10 ÷ 4
A1 for 2.5 m/s²

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Calculate the deceleration of the cyclist between 10 s and 12 s, in m/s².

markingPoints.text: C1 for 10 ÷ 2
A1 for 5.0 m/s²

parts.examinerComment: Give the deceleration as a positive value.

questions.stem: Fig. 3 shows a parallel circuit.

figures.alt: Circuit diagram: a 6.0 V cell with an ammeter in the main circuit, connected to a 3.0 Ω resistor and a 6.0 Ω resistor in parallel.
figures.caption: Fig. 3

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Calculate the current in the 3.0 Ω resistor, in A.

markingPoints.text: C1 for the p.d. across each branch is 6.0 V
A1 for 2.0 A

parts.examinerComment: Each parallel branch has the full supply voltage.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Calculate the reading on the ammeter, in A.

markingPoints.text: C1 for 2.0 A + 1.0 A
A1 for 3.0 A

parts.examinerComment: The current in the main circuit is the sum of the branch currents.

parts.prompt: A student uses a stopwatch to time 20 complete swings of a pendulum. The total time is {=20*P} s. What is the period of the pendulum?

markingPoints.text: A – {P} s

parts.examinerComment: The period is the time for one complete swing: divide the total time by the number of swings. Timing many swings reduces the effect of reaction time.

parts.prompt: Which list contains only scalar quantities?

markingPoints.text: C – distance, speed, energy

parts.examinerComment: Scalars have magnitude only. Displacement, force, velocity and acceleration all have a direction, so they are vectors.

parts.prompt: A measuring cylinder contains {V1} cm³ of water. A small stone is lowered into the water and the reading rises to {=V1+dV} cm³. What is the volume of the stone?

markingPoints.text: D – {dV} cm³

parts.examinerComment: The volume of the stone equals the volume of water it displaces: the final reading minus the starting reading.

parts.prompt: A runner's distance–time graph is a straight line sloping upwards. What does this show?

options.text: The runner is moving at constant speed.

markingPoints.text: B – The runner is moving at constant speed.

parts.examinerComment: A constant gradient on a distance–time graph means a constant speed. A curve would show a changing speed.

parts.prompt: A cyclist travels {=s1*t1} m in {t1} s and then {=s2*t2} m in the next {t2} s. What is her average speed for the whole journey?
parts.examinerComment: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time. Averaging the two speeds only works when the two times are equal.

parts.prompt: Which quantity is represented by the area under a speed–time graph?

markingPoints.text: C – distance travelled

parts.examinerComment: Area = speed × time = distance. The gradient of a speed–time graph gives the acceleration.

parts.prompt: What is meant by the mass of an object?

options.text: the gravitational force acting on the object
the quantity of matter in the object
the space occupied by the object
the mass of each unit of volume of the object

markingPoints.text: B – the quantity of matter in the object

parts.examinerComment: Mass is the quantity of matter. Weight is the gravitational force, and mass per unit volume is density.

parts.prompt: An object weighs {=m*g} N on a planet where the gravitational field strength is {g} N/kg. What is its mass?

markingPoints.text: C – {m} kg

parts.examinerComment: m = W ÷ g, using the field strength of the planet the object is on, not the value for the Earth.

parts.prompt: Which instrument measures the weight of an object directly?

markingPoints.text: B – a force meter (newton meter)

parts.examinerComment: A force meter measures a force in newtons. A beam balance compares masses.

parts.prompt: A liquid has a density of {rho} g/cm³. What is the mass of {V} cm³ of the liquid?

markingPoints.text: C – {=round(rho*V,2)} g

parts.examinerComment: m = ρ × V. Check that the units cancel: g/cm³ × cm³ = g.

parts.prompt: A solid block floats in water. What can be concluded about the block?

options.text: Its density is greater than the density of water.
Its mass is less than the mass of the water in the container.
Its density is less than the density of water.
Its weight is less than 1 N.

markingPoints.text: C – Its density is less than the density of water.

parts.examinerComment: Whether an object floats depends on its density compared with the liquid, not on its mass or weight.

parts.prompt: Which apparatus is needed to find the density of a rectangular wooden block?

markingPoints.text: C – a balance and a ruler

parts.examinerComment: The balance gives the mass. The ruler gives the three dimensions, which are multiplied to find the volume.

parts.prompt: A car moves at a constant velocity along a straight, level road. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The driving force is greater than the total resistive force.
There are no forces acting on the car.
The resultant force acts in the direction of motion.
The driving force is equal to the total resistive force.

markingPoints.text: D – The driving force is equal to the total resistive force.

parts.examinerComment: Constant velocity means zero acceleration, so the resultant force is zero: the forces are balanced.

parts.prompt: Two forces act on a box along the same straight line: {F1} N to the left and {F2} N to the right. What is the resultant force on the box?

markingPoints.text: A – {=F2-F1} N to the right

parts.examinerComment: Forces in opposite directions are subtracted. The resultant acts in the direction of the larger force.

parts.prompt: A uniform metre rule is balanced at its centre. A {W1} N weight hangs {d1} cm to the left of the pivot. Where must a {=2*W1} N weight be hung for the rule to balance?

options.text: {d1} cm to the right of the pivot
{=2*d1} cm to the right of the pivot
{=d1/2} cm to the right of the pivot
{=d1/4} cm to the right of the pivot

markingPoints.text: C – {=d1/2} cm to the right of the pivot

parts.examinerComment: For balance the clockwise moment equals the anticlockwise moment. Doubling the weight halves the distance needed.

parts.prompt: A ball is thrown vertically upwards. Which energy transfer takes place as it rises?

options.text: gravitational potential store to kinetic store
kinetic store to gravitational potential store

markingPoints.text: C – kinetic store to gravitational potential store

parts.examinerComment: The ball slows down as it gains height, so energy is transferred from its kinetic store to its gravitational potential store.

parts.prompt: A motor does {=P*t} J of useful work in {t} s. What is its useful power output?

markingPoints.text: B – {P} W

parts.examinerComment: Power = work done ÷ time taken.

parts.prompt: Which energy resource is non-renewable?

markingPoints.text: C – natural gas

parts.examinerComment: Fossil fuels such as natural gas cannot be replaced once used. The others are continually replenished.

parts.prompt: Why does a sharp knife cut more easily than a blunt knife, when the same force is used?

options.text: The force acts on a larger area, giving a greater pressure.
The force acts on a smaller area, giving a greater pressure.
A sharp knife exerts a greater force.
The pressure is smaller, so the knife moves more easily.

markingPoints.text: B – The force acts on a smaller area, giving a greater pressure.

parts.examinerComment: p = F ÷ A. A smaller area gives a larger pressure for the same force.

parts.prompt: A pressure of {p} Pa acts on an area of {A} m². What is the force on the area?

markingPoints.text: C – {=round(p*A,4)} N

parts.examinerComment: F = p × A. Pressure in pascals is the force in newtons on each square metre.

parts.prompt: A diver swims deeper in a lake. What happens to the pressure on the diver, and why?

options.text: It decreases, because the water is colder.
It stays the same, because the density of water does not change.
It increases, because the diver's weight increases.
It increases, because there is a greater depth of water above the diver.

markingPoints.text: D – It increases, because there is a greater depth of water above the diver.

parts.examinerComment: Pressure in a liquid increases with depth because there is more liquid above pushing down.

parts.prompt: Which statement describes the particles in a solid?

options.text: far apart and moving randomly at high speed
close together and moving randomly past each other
closely packed in a regular pattern and vibrating about fixed positions
closely packed and not moving at all

markingPoints.text: C – closely packed in a regular pattern and vibrating about fixed positions

parts.examinerComment: Particles in a solid still vibrate. They cannot move from place to place, which is why a solid keeps its shape.

parts.prompt: Smoke particles in air are viewed through a microscope. They move about in a random, jerky way. What causes this motion?

options.text: collisions with fast-moving air molecules, which are too small to see
the smoke particles attracting each other
energy from the light of the microscope lamp

markingPoints.text: B – collisions with fast-moving air molecules, which are too small to see

parts.examinerComment: This is Brownian motion. The smoke particles are hit unevenly by many much smaller, fast-moving air molecules.

parts.prompt: A gas is heated in a sealed container of fixed volume. Why does its pressure increase?

options.text: The particles move faster and hit the walls more often and with more force.
The particles move more slowly and stick to the walls.

markingPoints.text: C – The particles move faster and hit the walls more often and with more force.

parts.examinerComment: Heating increases the average kinetic energy of the particles. The particles do not change size.

parts.prompt: Equal volumes of a solid, a liquid and a gas are heated through the same temperature rise at constant pressure. Which expands the most?

options.text: they all expand by the same amount

markingPoints.text: C – the gas

parts.examinerComment: Gases expand far more than liquids, which expand more than solids.

parts.prompt: What is the melting point of pure ice at standard atmospheric pressure?

markingPoints.text: B – 0 °C

parts.examinerComment: Pure water freezes and ice melts at 0 °C; pure water boils at 100 °C.

parts.prompt: Why does sweating help to keep the body cool?

options.text: Sweat is colder than the body.
Sweat reflects thermal radiation away from the skin.
The more energetic water molecules escape from the sweat, leaving the remaining liquid cooler.
Water conducts thermal energy into the body.

markingPoints.text: C – The more energetic water molecules escape from the sweat, leaving the remaining liquid cooler.

parts.examinerComment: Evaporation removes the most energetic particles, so the average kinetic energy of those left falls and the liquid cools the skin.

parts.prompt: The cooling fins on the back of a refrigerator are painted dull black. Why?

options.text: Dull black surfaces are good reflectors of infrared radiation.
Dull black surfaces are good emitters of infrared radiation.
Black paint is a good thermal conductor.

markingPoints.text: B – Dull black surfaces are good emitters of infrared radiation.

parts.examinerComment: Dull black surfaces are good absorbers and good emitters of infrared radiation.

parts.prompt: Which material is the best thermal conductor?

markingPoints.text: D – copper

parts.examinerComment: Metals are the best thermal conductors. Gases such as air are very poor conductors.

parts.prompt: A heater is placed near the floor of a cold room. How is thermal energy mainly transferred around the room?

options.text: by convection: cool air rises and warm air sinks
by convection: warm air rises and cooler air sinks

markingPoints.text: C – by convection: warm air rises and cooler air sinks

parts.examinerComment: Warm air expands, becomes less dense and rises. Cooler, denser air sinks to replace it.

parts.prompt: Water waves travel at {=lam*f} m/s and have a frequency of {f} Hz. What is their wavelength?

markingPoints.text: C – {lam} m

parts.examinerComment: λ = v ÷ f.

parts.prompt: Which type of wave is longitudinal?

markingPoints.text: B – sound

parts.examinerComment: In a sound wave the particles vibrate parallel to the direction of travel. Electromagnetic waves and water ripples are transverse.

parts.prompt: What is the amplitude of a wave?

options.text: the distance between two neighbouring crests
the distance between a crest and the next trough
the number of waves passing a point each second
the maximum displacement of a point from its rest position

markingPoints.text: D – the maximum displacement of a point from its rest position

parts.examinerComment: Amplitude is measured from the rest position to a crest, not from a crest to a trough.

parts.prompt: An object is placed {d} cm in front of a plane mirror. How far is the image from the object?

markingPoints.text: C – {=2*d} cm

parts.examinerComment: The image is as far behind the mirror as the object is in front, so the distance from object to image is twice the distance to the mirror.

parts.prompt: White light passes through a glass prism and is dispersed into a spectrum. Which colour is refracted the most?

markingPoints.text: D – violet

parts.examinerComment: Violet light is refracted most and red least. The order is red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet.

parts.prompt: What is the principal focus of a converging lens?

options.text: the point where rays parallel to the principal axis meet after passing through the lens
the point where the image is always formed
the distance between the lens and the image

markingPoints.text: B – the point where rays parallel to the principal axis meet after passing through the lens

parts.examinerComment: The focal length is the distance from the centre of the lens to the principal focus.

parts.prompt: Which list gives regions of the electromagnetic spectrum in order of increasing frequency?

options.text: visible light, infrared, microwaves, radio waves
radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light
X-rays, gamma rays, ultraviolet, visible light

markingPoints.text: B – radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light

parts.examinerComment: In order of increasing frequency: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma.

parts.prompt: Which type of electromagnetic radiation is used to sterilise medical equipment?

markingPoints.text: D – gamma rays

parts.examinerComment: Gamma rays are highly penetrating and kill bacteria, even through sealed packaging.

parts.prompt: Which property is the same for all electromagnetic waves in a vacuum?

markingPoints.text: C – speed

parts.examinerComment: All electromagnetic waves travel at the same high speed in a vacuum.

parts.prompt: A ship's sonar sends a pulse of ultrasound down to the sea bed. The echo returns {t} s later. The speed of sound in sea water is 1500 m/s. What is the depth of the sea?
parts.examinerComment: The pulse travels to the sea bed and back, so the depth is half of speed × time.

parts.prompt: Which statement about ultrasound is correct?

options.text: It has a frequency below 20 Hz.
It travels faster than audible sound in air.
It has a frequency above 20 kHz.

markingPoints.text: D – It has a frequency above 20 kHz.

parts.examinerComment: Ultrasound is sound above the range of human hearing (20 Hz to 20 kHz). It travels at the same speed as other sound in the same medium.

parts.prompt: A musical note becomes louder but its pitch stays the same. What has changed?

markingPoints.text: A – the amplitude has increased

parts.examinerComment: Loudness depends on amplitude; pitch depends on frequency.

parts.prompt: Which material is most suitable for the core of an electromagnet?

markingPoints.text: C – soft iron

parts.examinerComment: Soft iron is easily magnetised and loses its magnetism when the current is switched off.

parts.prompt: Which metal is not attracted by a magnet?

markingPoints.text: D – aluminium

parts.examinerComment: Iron, nickel and cobalt are ferrous (magnetic) materials. Aluminium is non-magnetic.

parts.prompt: How can a student tell whether a steel bar is a magnet or just an unmagnetised piece of steel?

options.text: Only a magnet is attracted to another magnet.
Only a magnet can repel another magnet.
Only an unmagnetised bar is attracted to a compass.

markingPoints.text: B – Only a magnet can repel another magnet.

parts.examinerComment: Both a magnet and a piece of magnetic material are attracted to a magnet. Only repulsion proves that the bar is a magnet.

parts.prompt: Two plastic rods are each rubbed with a cloth and both become negatively charged. What happens when they are brought close together?

options.text: There is no force between them.

markingPoints.text: B – They repel.

parts.examinerComment: Like charges repel. The rods became negative by gaining electrons from the cloth.

parts.prompt: There is a current of {I} A in a {R} Ω resistor. What is the potential difference across the resistor?

markingPoints.text: D – {=round(R*I,3)} V

parts.examinerComment: V = IR.

parts.prompt: What is the unit of potential difference?

markingPoints.text: B – volt

parts.examinerComment: Potential difference is measured in volts with a voltmeter connected in parallel.

parts.prompt: Two lamps are connected in parallel to a battery. The filament of one lamp breaks. What happens to the other lamp?

options.text: It goes out, because the circuit is broken.
It stays lit, because it is still in a complete circuit with the battery.
It goes out, because all the current went through the broken lamp.
It becomes much brighter than before.

markingPoints.text: B – It stays lit, because it is still in a complete circuit with the battery.

parts.examinerComment: Each branch of a parallel circuit is connected directly across the battery, so one branch does not depend on the other.

parts.prompt: Three cells, each of e.m.f. {e} V, are connected in series, all facing the same way. What is their combined e.m.f.?
parts.examinerComment: The e.m.f.s of cells connected in series in the same direction add together.

parts.prompt: A lamp and a resistor are connected in series to a power supply. The potential difference is {V1} V across the lamp and {V2} V across the resistor. What is the e.m.f. of the supply?
parts.examinerComment: In a series circuit, the potential differences across the components add up to the e.m.f. of the supply.

parts.prompt: In a mains plug, which wire is connected to the fuse?

markingPoints.text: A – live

parts.examinerComment: The fuse is in the live wire so that the appliance is disconnected from the high voltage when the fuse melts.

parts.prompt: Why is it dangerous to use mains electrical appliances with wet hands?

options.text: Water increases the resistance of the appliance.
Water reduces the current in the appliance.
Water can conduct electricity, increasing the risk of an electric shock.
Water makes the fuse melt more slowly.

markingPoints.text: C – Water can conduct electricity, increasing the risk of an electric shock.

parts.examinerComment: Damp conditions are one of the main hazards of mains electricity.

parts.prompt: What is the main hazard of a mains cable with damaged insulation?

options.text: A person could touch the exposed wire and receive an electric shock.

markingPoints.text: B – A person could touch the exposed wire and receive an electric shock.

parts.examinerComment: Damaged insulation can expose the live wire.

parts.prompt: A transformer has {=k*Ns} turns on its primary coil and {Ns} turns on its secondary coil. The primary voltage is {Vp} V. What is the secondary voltage?

markingPoints.text: B – {=round(Vp/k,2)} V

parts.examinerComment: Vp ÷ Vs = Np ÷ Ns. This is a step-down transformer, so the secondary voltage is smaller.

parts.prompt: Which change makes a simple d.c. motor turn faster?

options.text: increasing the current in the coil
using fewer turns on the coil

markingPoints.text: C – increasing the current in the coil

parts.examinerComment: Increasing the current, the number of turns or the strength of the magnetic field increases the turning effect.

parts.prompt: A wire connected to a sensitive voltmeter is moved quickly down between the poles of a magnet. What is observed?

options.text: A reading appears while the wire moves and returns to zero when it stops.
A steady reading that stays when the wire stops.
No reading, because there is no battery in the circuit.
A reading only when the wire is held still in the field.

markingPoints.text: A – A reading appears while the wire moves and returns to zero when it stops.

parts.examinerComment: An e.m.f. is induced only while the wire cuts through the magnetic field lines.

parts.prompt: A nucleus has a nucleon number of {=2*Z+d} and a proton number of {Z}. How many neutrons does it contain?
parts.examinerComment: Number of neutrons = nucleon number − proton number.

parts.prompt: Which particle has a negative charge?

markingPoints.text: A – electron

parts.examinerComment: Protons are positive and neutrons have no charge, so a nucleus is positive.

parts.prompt: What are isotopes of an element?

options.text: atoms with the same number of neutrons but different numbers of protons
atoms with the same nucleon number but different proton numbers
atoms with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons
atoms with the same number of protons but different numbers of electrons

markingPoints.text: C – atoms with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons

parts.examinerComment: Isotopes of an element have the same proton number but different nucleon numbers.

parts.prompt: Which type of radiation is stopped by a thin sheet of paper?

markingPoints.text: A – alpha

parts.examinerComment: Alpha particles have a short range. Beta is stopped by a few mm of aluminium; gamma is reduced by thick lead.

parts.prompt: The activity of a radioactive sample falls from {=k*2^n} Bq to {k} Bq in {=n*T} hours. What is the half-life of the sample?

markingPoints.text: A – {T} hours

parts.examinerComment: Halving {n} times takes {=k*2^n} Bq down to {k} Bq, so {n} half-lives last {=n*T} hours.

parts.prompt: Which is a source of background radiation?

markingPoints.text: B – radon gas from rocks

parts.examinerComment: Natural sources include radon gas, rocks and buildings, food and drink, and cosmic rays.

parts.prompt: What causes the seasons on the Earth?

options.text: The distance between the Earth and the Sun changes a lot during the year.
The Earth spins on its axis once every 24 hours.
The Earth's axis is tilted relative to the plane of its orbit around the Sun.
The Moon sometimes blocks light from the Sun.

markingPoints.text: C – The Earth's axis is tilted relative to the plane of its orbit around the Sun.

parts.examinerComment: When a hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun, the Sun is higher in the sky and days are longer, so it is summer there.

parts.prompt: A space probe is {d} × 10¹¹ m from the Earth. How long does a radio signal take to travel from the Earth to the probe? (speed of radio waves = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s)
parts.examinerComment: time = distance ÷ speed. Take care with the powers of ten.

parts.prompt: About how long does the Moon take to orbit the Earth once?

markingPoints.text: C – 1 month

parts.examinerComment: The Moon takes about one month (about 27 days) to orbit the Earth.

parts.prompt: What is the approximate diameter of the Milky Way galaxy?

markingPoints.text: B – 100 000 light-years

parts.examinerComment: The Milky Way is about 100 000 light-years across.

parts.prompt: A star is {n} light-years from the Earth. What is this distance in metres? (1 light-year = 9.5 × 10¹⁵ m)
parts.examinerComment: Multiply the number of light-years by the length of one light-year.

parts.prompt: What is the Sun mainly made of?

markingPoints.text: C – hydrogen and helium

parts.examinerComment: The Sun is a medium-sized star made mostly of hydrogen and helium.

parts.prompt: A student uses a stopwatch to time 20 complete swings of a pendulum. The total time is {=20*P} s. What is the period of the pendulum?

markingPoints.text: A – {P} s

parts.examinerComment: The period is the time for one complete swing: divide the total time by the number of swings. Timing many swings reduces the effect of reaction time.

parts.prompt: Which list contains only scalar quantities?

markingPoints.text: C – distance, speed, energy

parts.examinerComment: Scalars have magnitude only. Displacement, force, velocity and acceleration all have a direction, so they are vectors.

parts.prompt: Two forces of {=3*k} N and {=4*k} N act at right angles to each other on the same point. What is the magnitude of the resultant force?
parts.examinerComment: Forces at right angles combine by Pythagoras' theorem: √(({=3*k})² + ({=4*k})²). Simply adding the forces is only correct when they act in the same direction.

parts.prompt: A runner's distance–time graph is a straight line sloping upwards. What does this show?

options.text: The runner is moving at constant speed.

markingPoints.text: B – The runner is moving at constant speed.

parts.examinerComment: A constant gradient on a distance–time graph means a constant speed. A curve would show a changing speed.

parts.prompt: A cyclist travels {=s1*t1} m in {t1} s and then {=s2*t2} m in the next {t2} s. What is her average speed for the whole journey?
parts.examinerComment: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time. Averaging the two speeds only works when the two times are equal.

parts.prompt: A ball is dropped from a great height. Air resistance acts on it. Which statement describes its motion as it falls?

options.text: Its acceleration decreases until it reaches terminal velocity.
Its acceleration increases as its speed increases.
It falls with a constant acceleration of 9.8 m/s² throughout.
Its speed increases until air resistance is greater than its weight, and then it slows to a stop.

markingPoints.text: A – Its acceleration decreases until it reaches terminal velocity.

parts.examinerComment: Air resistance increases with speed, so the resultant force and the acceleration decrease. At terminal velocity the forces are balanced and the acceleration is zero.

parts.prompt: What is meant by the mass of an object?

options.text: the gravitational force acting on the object
the quantity of matter in the object
the space occupied by the object
the mass of each unit of volume of the object

markingPoints.text: B – the quantity of matter in the object

parts.examinerComment: Mass is the quantity of matter. Weight is the gravitational force, and mass per unit volume is density.

parts.prompt: An object weighs {=m*g} N on a planet where the gravitational field strength is {g} N/kg. What is its mass?

markingPoints.text: C – {m} kg

parts.examinerComment: m = W ÷ g, using the field strength of the planet the object is on, not the value for the Earth.

parts.prompt: What is the gravitational field strength at a point?

options.text: the force per unit mass on a mass placed at that point
the force per unit charge on a charge placed at that point
the mass per unit volume of the planet
the energy per unit mass of an object at that point

markingPoints.text: A – the force per unit mass on a mass placed at that point

parts.examinerComment: g = W ÷ m, measured in N/kg. It is numerically equal to the acceleration of free fall.

parts.prompt: A liquid has a density of {rho} g/cm³. What is the mass of {V} cm³ of the liquid?

markingPoints.text: C – {=round(rho*V,2)} g

parts.examinerComment: m = ρ × V. Check that the units cancel: g/cm³ × cm³ = g.

parts.prompt: A solid block floats in water. What can be concluded about the block?

options.text: Its density is greater than the density of water.
Its mass is less than the mass of the water in the container.
Its density is less than the density of water.
Its weight is less than 1 N.

markingPoints.text: C – Its density is less than the density of water.

parts.examinerComment: Whether an object floats depends on its density compared with the liquid, not on its mass or weight.

parts.prompt: Three liquids that do not mix are poured into a tall jar: oil (density 0.92 g/cm³), water (1.00 g/cm³) and syrup (1.33 g/cm³). In which order do the layers settle, from top to bottom?

markingPoints.text: D – oil, water, syrup

parts.examinerComment: A less dense liquid floats on a denser one, so the least dense liquid forms the top layer.

parts.prompt: A car moves at a constant velocity along a straight, level road. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The driving force is greater than the total resistive force.
There are no forces acting on the car.
The resultant force acts in the direction of motion.
The driving force is equal to the total resistive force.

markingPoints.text: D – The driving force is equal to the total resistive force.

parts.examinerComment: Constant velocity means zero acceleration, so the resultant force is zero: the forces are balanced.

parts.prompt: Two forces act on a box along the same straight line: {F1} N to the left and {F2} N to the right. What is the resultant force on the box?

markingPoints.text: A – {=F2-F1} N to the right

parts.examinerComment: Forces in opposite directions are subtracted. The resultant acts in the direction of the larger force.

parts.prompt: An object moves in a horizontal circle at constant speed. Which statement about the resultant force on the object is correct?

options.text: It is zero, because the speed is constant.
It acts in the direction of motion.
It acts outwards, away from the centre of the circle.
It acts towards the centre of the circle, at right angles to the motion.

markingPoints.text: D – It acts towards the centre of the circle, at right angles to the motion.

parts.examinerComment: The direction of the velocity is always changing, so there must be a resultant force. It acts at right angles to the motion, towards the centre.

parts.prompt: Which is a correct unit for impulse?

markingPoints.text: B – N s

parts.examinerComment: Impulse = force × time, so its unit is N s, which is the same as kg m/s, the unit of momentum.

parts.prompt: A ball of mass {m} kg moving at {u} m/s hits a wall and rebounds along the same line at {v} m/s. What is the magnitude of the change in momentum of the ball?

markingPoints.text: D – {=round(m*(u+v),3)} kg m/s

parts.examinerComment: Momentum is a vector. When the ball rebounds its velocity changes sign, so the change is m(u + v).

parts.prompt: A ball is thrown vertically upwards. Which energy transfer takes place as it rises?

options.text: gravitational potential store to kinetic store
kinetic store to gravitational potential store

markingPoints.text: C – kinetic store to gravitational potential store

parts.examinerComment: The ball slows down as it gains height, so energy is transferred from its kinetic store to its gravitational potential store.

parts.prompt: A motor does {=P*t} J of useful work in {t} s. What is its useful power output?

markingPoints.text: B – {P} W

parts.examinerComment: Power = work done ÷ time taken.

parts.prompt: A lamp is supplied with {E} J of electrical energy each second and emits {=e*E/100} J of light energy each second. What is its efficiency?
parts.examinerComment: Efficiency = useful energy output ÷ total energy input × 100%. An efficiency can never be more than 100%.

parts.prompt: Which is the original source of the energy in coal, wind and hydroelectric resources?

markingPoints.text: A – the Sun

parts.examinerComment: Radiation from the Sun grew the plants that formed coal, causes winds and evaporates water. Geothermal, nuclear and tidal resources do not come from the Sun.

parts.prompt: Why does a sharp knife cut more easily than a blunt knife, when the same force is used?

options.text: The force acts on a larger area, giving a greater pressure.
The force acts on a smaller area, giving a greater pressure.
A sharp knife exerts a greater force.
The pressure is smaller, so the knife moves more easily.

markingPoints.text: B – The force acts on a smaller area, giving a greater pressure.

parts.examinerComment: p = F ÷ A. A smaller area gives a larger pressure for the same force.

parts.prompt: A pressure of {p} Pa acts on an area of {A} m². What is the force on the area?

markingPoints.text: C – {=round(p*A,4)} N

parts.examinerComment: F = p × A. Pressure in pascals is the force in newtons on each square metre.

parts.prompt: What is the pressure due to a column of liquid of density {rho} kg/m³ and depth {h} m? (g = 9.8 N/kg)

markingPoints.text: B – {=round(rho*9.8*h,3)} Pa

parts.examinerComment: Δp = ρgΔh. All three quantities are multiplied.

parts.prompt: Which statement describes the particles in a solid?

options.text: far apart and moving randomly at high speed
close together and moving randomly past each other
closely packed in a regular pattern and vibrating about fixed positions
closely packed and not moving at all

markingPoints.text: C – closely packed in a regular pattern and vibrating about fixed positions

parts.examinerComment: Particles in a solid still vibrate. They cannot move from place to place, which is why a solid keeps its shape.

parts.prompt: Smoke particles in air are viewed through a microscope. They move about in a random, jerky way. What causes this motion?

options.text: collisions with fast-moving air molecules, which are too small to see
the smoke particles attracting each other
energy from the light of the microscope lamp

markingPoints.text: B – collisions with fast-moving air molecules, which are too small to see

parts.examinerComment: This is Brownian motion. The smoke particles are hit unevenly by many much smaller, fast-moving air molecules.

parts.prompt: What is a temperature of {c} °C on the kelvin scale?
parts.examinerComment: T (in K) = θ (in °C) + 273. A temperature in kelvin is never negative.

parts.prompt: Equal volumes of a solid, a liquid and a gas are heated through the same temperature rise at constant pressure. Which expands the most?

options.text: they all expand by the same amount

markingPoints.text: C – the gas

parts.examinerComment: Gases expand far more than liquids, which expand more than solids.

parts.prompt: What is the melting point of pure ice at standard atmospheric pressure?

markingPoints.text: B – 0 °C

parts.examinerComment: Pure water freezes and ice melts at 0 °C; pure water boils at 100 °C.

parts.prompt: {=c*m*dT} J of energy raises the temperature of {m} kg of a metal by {dT} °C. What is the specific heat capacity of the metal?

markingPoints.text: B – {c} J/(kg °C)

parts.examinerComment: c = ΔE ÷ (mΔθ). Dividing by only one of mass and temperature change is a common error.

parts.prompt: The cooling fins on the back of a refrigerator are painted dull black. Why?

options.text: Dull black surfaces are good reflectors of infrared radiation.
Dull black surfaces are good emitters of infrared radiation.
Black paint is a good thermal conductor.

markingPoints.text: B – Dull black surfaces are good emitters of infrared radiation.

parts.examinerComment: Dull black surfaces are good absorbers and good emitters of infrared radiation.

parts.prompt: Which material is the best thermal conductor?

markingPoints.text: D – copper

parts.examinerComment: Metals are the best thermal conductors. Gases such as air are very poor conductors.

parts.prompt: Why are metals much better thermal conductors than non-metals?

options.text: Metal atoms vibrate faster than non-metal atoms at the same temperature.
Metals contain free electrons, which transfer energy quickly through the metal.
Metals are less dense, so their particles move more freely.

markingPoints.text: B – Metals contain free electrons, which transfer energy quickly through the metal.

parts.examinerComment: In metals, free (delocalised) electrons carry energy quickly. Lattice vibrations also transfer energy, but much more slowly.

parts.prompt: Water waves travel at {=lam*f} m/s and have a frequency of {f} Hz. What is their wavelength?

markingPoints.text: C – {lam} m

parts.examinerComment: λ = v ÷ f.

parts.prompt: Which type of wave is longitudinal?

markingPoints.text: B – sound

parts.examinerComment: In a sound wave the particles vibrate parallel to the direction of travel. Electromagnetic waves and water ripples are transverse.

parts.prompt: Straight water waves pass through a gap in a barrier. Which change produces the greatest diffraction?

options.text: making the gap much wider than the wavelength
making the gap about the same size as the wavelength
increasing the amplitude of the waves
decreasing the wavelength, keeping the gap the same

markingPoints.text: B – making the gap about the same size as the wavelength

parts.examinerComment: Diffraction is most noticeable when the gap is similar in size to the wavelength.

parts.prompt: An object is placed {d} cm in front of a plane mirror. How far is the image from the object?

markingPoints.text: C – {=2*d} cm

parts.examinerComment: The image is as far behind the mirror as the object is in front, so the distance from object to image is twice the distance to the mirror.

parts.prompt: White light passes through a glass prism and is dispersed into a spectrum. Which colour is refracted the most?

markingPoints.text: D – violet

parts.examinerComment: Violet light is refracted most and red least. The order is red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet.

parts.prompt: A type of glass has a refractive index of {n}. What is the critical angle for light travelling from this glass into air?

markingPoints.text: A – {=round(asin(1/n)*180/pi,1)}°

parts.examinerComment: sin c = 1 ÷ n. Make sure the calculator is in degree mode.

parts.prompt: Which list gives regions of the electromagnetic spectrum in order of increasing frequency?

options.text: visible light, infrared, microwaves, radio waves
radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light
X-rays, gamma rays, ultraviolet, visible light

markingPoints.text: B – radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light

parts.examinerComment: In order of increasing frequency: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma.

parts.prompt: Which type of electromagnetic radiation is used to sterilise medical equipment?

markingPoints.text: D – gamma rays

parts.examinerComment: Gamma rays are highly penetrating and kill bacteria, even through sealed packaging.

parts.prompt: Microwaves have a wavelength of {lam} cm. What is their frequency? (speed of electromagnetic waves = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s)

markingPoints.text: B – {=round(30/lam,3)} × 10⁹ Hz

parts.examinerComment: f = v ÷ λ, with the wavelength converted to metres first.

parts.prompt: Why are microwaves used for communication with satellites?

options.text: They pass through the Earth's atmosphere without being significantly absorbed or reflected.
They diffract around the curved surface of the Earth.
They travel faster than other electromagnetic waves.
They are reflected by the ionosphere.

markingPoints.text: A – They pass through the Earth's atmosphere without being significantly absorbed or reflected.

parts.examinerComment: Microwaves pass through the atmosphere, so they can reach satellites. All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum.

parts.prompt: A ship's sonar sends a pulse of ultrasound down to the sea bed. The echo returns {t} s later. The speed of sound in sea water is 1500 m/s. What is the depth of the sea?
parts.examinerComment: The pulse travels to the sea bed and back, so the depth is half of speed × time.

parts.prompt: Which statement about ultrasound is correct?

options.text: It has a frequency below 20 Hz.
It travels faster than audible sound in air.
It has a frequency above 20 kHz.

markingPoints.text: D – It has a frequency above 20 kHz.

parts.examinerComment: Ultrasound is sound above the range of human hearing (20 Hz to 20 kHz). It travels at the same speed as other sound in the same medium.

parts.prompt: In which material does sound travel fastest?

markingPoints.text: C – steel

parts.examinerComment: Sound generally travels fastest in solids and slowest in gases. It cannot travel through a vacuum.

parts.prompt: Which material is most suitable for the core of an electromagnet?

markingPoints.text: C – soft iron

parts.examinerComment: Soft iron is easily magnetised and loses its magnetism when the current is switched off.

parts.prompt: Which metal is not attracted by a magnet?

markingPoints.text: D – aluminium

parts.examinerComment: Iron, nickel and cobalt are ferrous (magnetic) materials. Aluminium is non-magnetic.

parts.prompt: What does the spacing of magnetic field lines show?

options.text: the relative strength of the field: the closer the lines, the stronger the field
the direction of the force on a south pole
the relative strength of the field: the closer the lines, the weaker the field
the speed at which the field moves

markingPoints.text: A – the relative strength of the field: the closer the lines, the stronger the field

parts.examinerComment: The field is strongest where the lines are closest together, for example near the poles of a bar magnet.

parts.prompt: Two plastic rods are each rubbed with a cloth and both become negatively charged. What happens when they are brought close together?

options.text: There is no force between them.

markingPoints.text: B – They repel.

parts.examinerComment: Like charges repel. The rods became negative by gaining electrons from the cloth.

parts.prompt: There is a current of {I} A in a {R} Ω resistor. What is the potential difference across the resistor?

markingPoints.text: D – {=round(R*I,3)} V

parts.examinerComment: V = IR.

parts.prompt: A charge of {=I*t} C passes a point in a circuit in {t} s. What is the current?

markingPoints.text: C – {I} A

parts.examinerComment: I = Q ÷ t.

parts.prompt: Two lamps are connected in parallel to a battery. The filament of one lamp breaks. What happens to the other lamp?

options.text: It goes out, because the circuit is broken.
It stays lit, because it is still in a complete circuit with the battery.
It goes out, because all the current went through the broken lamp.
It becomes much brighter than before.

markingPoints.text: B – It stays lit, because it is still in a complete circuit with the battery.

parts.examinerComment: Each branch of a parallel circuit is connected directly across the battery, so one branch does not depend on the other.

parts.prompt: Three cells, each of e.m.f. {e} V, are connected in series, all facing the same way. What is their combined e.m.f.?
parts.examinerComment: The e.m.f.s of cells connected in series in the same direction add together.

parts.prompt: A {Vs} V supply is connected across a {R1} kΩ resistor and a {R2} kΩ resistor in series. What is the potential difference across the {R2} kΩ resistor?

markingPoints.text: B – {=round(Vs*R2/(R1+R2),2)} V

parts.examinerComment: In a potential divider the p.d. is shared in the ratio of the resistances: the larger resistor has the larger share.

parts.prompt: The light falling on a light-dependent resistor (LDR) becomes brighter. What happens to the resistance of the LDR?

options.text: It falls to zero and then increases.

markingPoints.text: B – It decreases.

parts.examinerComment: The resistance of an LDR decreases as light intensity increases.

parts.prompt: In a mains plug, which wire is connected to the fuse?

markingPoints.text: A – live

parts.examinerComment: The fuse is in the live wire so that the appliance is disconnected from the high voltage when the fuse melts.

parts.prompt: Why is it dangerous to use mains electrical appliances with wet hands?

options.text: Water increases the resistance of the appliance.
Water reduces the current in the appliance.
Water can conduct electricity, increasing the risk of an electric shock.
Water makes the fuse melt more slowly.

markingPoints.text: C – Water can conduct electricity, increasing the risk of an electric shock.

parts.examinerComment: Damp conditions are one of the main hazards of mains electricity.

parts.prompt: A hairdryer has a power of {P} W and is connected to the 230 V mains supply. What is the current in the hairdryer?

markingPoints.text: B – {=round(P/230,2)} A

parts.examinerComment: I = P ÷ V. The fuse chosen must have a rating just above this current.

parts.prompt: A transformer has {=k*Ns} turns on its primary coil and {Ns} turns on its secondary coil. The primary voltage is {Vp} V. What is the secondary voltage?

markingPoints.text: B – {=round(Vp/k,2)} V

parts.examinerComment: Vp ÷ Vs = Np ÷ Ns. This is a step-down transformer, so the secondary voltage is smaller.

parts.prompt: Which change makes a simple d.c. motor turn faster?

options.text: increasing the current in the coil
using fewer turns on the coil

markingPoints.text: C – increasing the current in the coil

parts.examinerComment: Increasing the current, the number of turns or the strength of the magnetic field increases the turning effect.

parts.prompt: What is the purpose of the slip rings and brushes in an a.c. generator?

options.text: to reverse the current every half turn so that the output is d.c.
to connect the rotating coil to the external circuit without twisting the wires
to increase the strength of the magnetic field
to slow down the rotation of the coil

markingPoints.text: B – to connect the rotating coil to the external circuit without twisting the wires

parts.examinerComment: Slip rings keep a continuous connection to the rotating coil. A split-ring commutator would reverse the connections.

parts.prompt: A nucleus has a nucleon number of {=2*Z+d} and a proton number of {Z}. How many neutrons does it contain?
parts.examinerComment: Number of neutrons = nucleon number − proton number.

parts.prompt: Which particle has a negative charge?

markingPoints.text: A – electron

parts.examinerComment: Protons are positive and neutrons have no charge, so a nucleus is positive.

parts.prompt: In the alpha-particle scattering experiment, a very small fraction of alpha particles were deflected through large angles. What does this show?

options.text: The positive charge and most of the mass of an atom are concentrated in a tiny nucleus.
Electrons are much lighter than alpha particles.
Positive charge is spread evenly throughout the atom.

markingPoints.text: A – The positive charge and most of the mass of an atom are concentrated in a tiny nucleus.

parts.examinerComment: Only a small, massive, positively charged nucleus could repel a few alpha particles through large angles.

parts.prompt: Which type of radiation is stopped by a thin sheet of paper?

markingPoints.text: A – alpha

parts.examinerComment: Alpha particles have a short range. Beta is stopped by a few mm of aluminium; gamma is reduced by thick lead.

parts.prompt: The activity of a radioactive sample falls from {=k*2^n} Bq to {k} Bq in {=n*T} hours. What is the half-life of the sample?

markingPoints.text: A – {T} hours

parts.examinerComment: Halving {n} times takes {=k*2^n} Bq down to {k} Bq, so {n} half-lives last {=n*T} hours.

parts.prompt: What is emitted in beta decay, and what change takes place in the nucleus?

options.text: an electron; a proton changes into a neutron
an electron; a neutron changes into a proton
a helium nucleus; the proton number decreases by 2
an electromagnetic wave; the nucleon number decreases by 1

markingPoints.text: B – an electron; a neutron changes into a proton

parts.examinerComment: In beta decay a neutron changes into a proton and a fast electron, so the proton number increases by 1.

parts.prompt: A detector near a source records {m} counts/minute. The background count rate is {b} counts/minute. What will the detector record after two half-lives of the source?

markingPoints.text: C – {=(m-b)/4+b} counts/minute

parts.examinerComment: Only the count rate from the source halves. Subtract the background, divide by 4, then add the background back.

parts.prompt: What causes the seasons on the Earth?

options.text: The distance between the Earth and the Sun changes a lot during the year.
The Earth spins on its axis once every 24 hours.
The Earth's axis is tilted relative to the plane of its orbit around the Sun.
The Moon sometimes blocks light from the Sun.

markingPoints.text: C – The Earth's axis is tilted relative to the plane of its orbit around the Sun.

parts.examinerComment: When a hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun, the Sun is higher in the sky and days are longer, so it is summer there.

parts.prompt: A space probe is {d} × 10¹¹ m from the Earth. How long does a radio signal take to travel from the Earth to the probe? (speed of radio waves = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s)
parts.examinerComment: time = distance ÷ speed. Take care with the powers of ten.

parts.prompt: A comet moves in an elliptical orbit around the Sun. What happens to its speed as it moves closer to the Sun?

markingPoints.text: A – It increases.

parts.examinerComment: Gravitational potential energy is transferred to kinetic energy as the comet approaches the Sun.

parts.prompt: What is the approximate diameter of the Milky Way galaxy?

markingPoints.text: B – 100 000 light-years

parts.examinerComment: The Milky Way is about 100 000 light-years across.

parts.prompt: A star is {n} light-years from the Earth. What is this distance in metres? (1 light-year = 9.5 × 10¹⁵ m)
parts.examinerComment: Multiply the number of light-years by the length of one light-year.

parts.prompt: What can remain after a star much more massive than the Sun explodes as a supernova?

options.text: a neutron star or a black hole

markingPoints.text: C – a neutron star or a black hole

parts.examinerComment: Stars like the Sun end as white dwarfs. The cores of much more massive stars become neutron stars or black holes.

parts.prompt: A galaxy is {d} × 10²⁴ m from the Earth. The Hubble constant is 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹. What is the speed at which the galaxy is moving away?
parts.examinerComment: v = H₀d. Multiply the numbers and add the powers of ten: 10⁻¹⁸ × 10²⁴ = 10⁶.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: A student lays {n} identical coins edge to edge in a straight row. The row is {=round(n*d,2)} cm long. Calculate the diameter of one coin, in cm.

markingPoints.text: C1 for diameter = total length ÷ number of coins
A1 for {=round(round(n*d,2)/n,3)} cm

parts.examinerComment: Well answered. A few candidates multiplied instead of dividing.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Explain why measuring the length of a row of many coins gives a more accurate value for the diameter of one coin than measuring a single coin.

markingPoints.text: the uncertainty in reading the ruler (about 1 mm) is the same whatever length is measured
dividing by the number of coins divides the uncertainty too / the percentage uncertainty is much smaller

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers referred to the uncertainty in each ruler reading rather than simply saying the result is 'more accurate'.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: State the name of the piece of laboratory apparatus normally used to measure the volume of a liquid.

markingPoints.text: measuring cylinder

parts.examinerComment: Read the scale at the bottom of the meniscus with the eye level with the liquid surface.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: The period of a pendulum is about 1 s. Describe how a student can use a stopwatch to obtain an accurate value for the period.

markingPoints.text: time a large number of oscillations, e.g. 20
divide the total time by the number of oscillations
repeat the measurement and calculate an average
use a reference marker at the centre of the swing to start and stop timing

parts.examinerComment: Many candidates timed a single swing. Human reaction time is about 0.2 s, which is a large fraction of 1 s.

questions.stem: A car is driven along a straight road.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: A car travels at a constant speed of {v} m/s for {t} s. Calculate the distance travelled, in m.

markingPoints.text: C1 for distance = speed × time
A1 for {=v*t} m

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A car slows down uniformly from {u} m/s to rest in {t} s. Calculate its deceleration, in m/s².

markingPoints.text: C1 for a = change in speed ÷ time
A1 for {=round(u/t,3)} m/s²

parts.examinerComment: Most candidates divided correctly. A deceleration is given as a positive number.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Describe the shape of the distance–time graph for a car that is slowing down to a stop.

markingPoints.text: a curve (not a straight line)
the gradient decreases / the curve becomes less steep
the line becomes horizontal (gradient zero) when the car has stopped

parts.examinerComment: Weaker answers described a speed–time graph instead. Read the axes in the question carefully.

questions.stem: An astronaut brings rock samples from the Moon back to the Earth.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: State whether the mass and the weight of the rock change when it is brought to the Earth. Explain your answers.

markingPoints.text: mass stays the same
because the amount of matter in the rock does not change
weight increases
because the gravitational field strength on Earth is greater than on the Moon

parts.examinerComment: Many candidates said the mass increases. Mass depends only on the amount of matter, not on where the object is.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A rock sample has a mass of {m} kg. Calculate its weight on the Earth, in N. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

markingPoints.text: C1 for W = mg
A1 for {=round(m*9.8,3)} N

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: A different rock weighs {W} N on the Moon, where the gravitational field strength is 1.6 N/kg. Calculate its mass, in kg.

markingPoints.text: C1 for m = W ÷ g
A1 for {=round(W/1.6,3)} kg

parts.examinerComment: Some candidates used 9.8 N/kg; the weight was measured on the Moon, so the Moon's value is needed.

questions.stem: A student measures the densities of some solid objects.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: The water level in a measuring cylinder rises from {V1} cm³ to {=V1+dV} cm³ when a piece of metal is lowered into it. The mass of the metal is {=rho*dV} g. Calculate the density of the metal, in g/cm³.

markingPoints.text: C1 for volume = {=V1+dV} − {V1} = {dV} cm³
C1 for density = mass ÷ volume
A1 for {rho} g/cm³

parts.examinerComment: A common error was to divide the mass by the final reading rather than by the change in reading.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Suggest one precaution the student should take when lowering the metal into the measuring cylinder, and explain why it is needed.

markingPoints.text: lower the metal gently on a thread / tilt the cylinder and slide it in
so that no water splashes out (which would make the volume reading too small)
or: read the scale at eye level at the bottom of the meniscus to avoid parallax error

parts.examinerComment: Answers needed both the precaution and its effect on the measurement.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: A wooden block measures {a} cm × {b} cm × {c} cm and has a mass of {=round(rho*a*b*c,2)} g. Calculate the density of the wood, in g/cm³.

markingPoints.text: C1 for volume = {a} × {b} × {c} = {=a*b*c} cm³
A1 for {rho} g/cm³

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: The density of water is 1.0 g/cm³. State whether a block of wood of density 0.6 g/cm³ floats or sinks in water.

markingPoints.text: floats (its density is less than that of water)

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

questions.stem: This question is about the effects of forces.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: The unstretched length of a spring is {L0} cm. When a load is hung from it, its length becomes {=L0+e} cm. Calculate the extension of the spring, in cm.

markingPoints.text: B1 for {=L0+e} − {L0} = {e} cm

parts.examinerComment: The extension is the increase in length, not the new length.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Describe how a load–extension graph shows whether the spring has been stretched beyond its limit of proportionality.

markingPoints.text: up to the limit the graph is a straight line through the origin (extension proportional to load)
beyond the limit the graph curves / is no longer a straight line

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers described both parts of the graph.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: A seesaw is pivoted at its centre. A child of weight {W1} N sits {d1} m from the pivot. Calculate how far from the pivot a child of weight {W2} N must sit on the other side to balance the seesaw, in m.

markingPoints.text: C1 for clockwise moment = anticlockwise moment
A1 for {=round(W1*d1/W2,3)} m

parts.examinerComment: Most candidates applied the principle of moments correctly. Moments use the perpendicular distance from the pivot.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Explain why a racing car is designed with a wide wheelbase and a low centre of gravity.

markingPoints.text: the car is more stable / less likely to topple over (when cornering)
the line of action of its weight stays inside the base (between the wheels) even when the car tilts

parts.examinerComment: Answers needed to refer to the position of the centre of gravity relative to the base.

questions.stem: A crane is used on a building site.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: A crane lifts a load of weight {W} N through a vertical height of {h} m. Calculate the work done on the load, in J.

markingPoints.text: C1 for work done = force × distance
A1 for {=W*h} J

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: The crane's motor does {=P*t} J of work in {t} s. Calculate the power of the motor, in W.

markingPoints.text: C1 for power = work done ÷ time
A1 for {P} W
