parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Describe the main energy transfers when the crane's electric motor lifts the load. Explain why the energy supplied to the motor is greater than the energy gained by the load.

markingPoints.text: energy is transferred electrically to the motor
energy is transferred to the gravitational potential store of the load
some energy is dissipated to the thermal store of the surroundings (and as sound)
because of friction in the moving parts / resistance in the wires

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers named stores and explained where the wasted energy goes.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of using wind turbines to generate electricity.

markingPoints.text: advantage: renewable / no fuel cost / no carbon dioxide or polluting gases produced while operating
disadvantage: output depends on the wind and is unreliable / noisy / visual impact / needs a large area

parts.examinerComment: 'Wind is free' is acceptable for the advantage; 'it is bad for the environment' is too vague.

questions.stem: This question is about pressure.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: A woman of weight {W} N stands on both feet. The total area of her shoes in contact with the floor is {A} m². Calculate the pressure she exerts on the floor, in Pa.

markingPoints.text: C1 for p = F ÷ A
A1 for {=round(W/A,1)} Pa

parts.examinerComment: Well answered. A few candidates multiplied the force by the area.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: She then puts on shoes with narrow stiletto heels. Explain why these heels may damage a wooden floor.

markingPoints.text: her weight / the force on the floor is the same
the area in contact is much smaller, so the pressure is much greater

parts.examinerComment: Answers that said the force increases did not gain credit.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: The wall of a dam is much thicker at the bottom than at the top. Explain why.

markingPoints.text: pressure in water increases with depth
so the force on the bottom of the wall is greater and it must be stronger there

parts.examinerComment: Most candidates knew that pressure increases with depth.

questions.stem: This question is about the particle model of matter.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Describe the differences in the arrangement and motion of the particles in liquid water and in steam.

markingPoints.text: in the liquid the particles are close together / touching
in steam the particles are far apart
in the liquid the particles move around / slide past each other
in steam the particles move randomly at high speed

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers compared both arrangement and motion for both states.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Explain, in terms of particles, why a gas exerts a pressure on the walls of its container.

markingPoints.text: the particles collide with the walls
each collision exerts a force on the wall, and pressure is the force per unit area

parts.examinerComment: Collisions between particles do not produce the pressure on the walls; the collisions with the walls do.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: A sealed balloon filled with air is put in a freezer. State what happens to the volume of the balloon and explain why, in terms of the particles.

markingPoints.text: the volume decreases
the particles move more slowly / have less kinetic energy
they hit the inside of the balloon less often and with less force
so the pressure inside falls and the balloon shrinks

parts.examinerComment: The particles do not shrink; the space between them changes.

questions.stem: This question is about thermal properties of water and other substances.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Describe evaporation in terms of particles.

markingPoints.text: the more energetic particles escape
from the surface of the liquid (at temperatures below the boiling point)

parts.examinerComment: Weaker answers described boiling. Evaporation happens only at the surface.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: State the boiling point of pure water at standard atmospheric pressure, in °C.

markingPoints.text: B1 for 100 °C

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Explain how a liquid-in-glass thermometer uses thermal expansion to show the temperature.

markingPoints.text: the liquid expands when it is heated (more than the glass)
so it rises up the narrow tube and its level is read against the scale

parts.examinerComment: Most candidates knew that the liquid expands.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Ice at 0 °C is heated and melts. Explain why its temperature stays at 0 °C while it is melting, even though it is being heated.

markingPoints.text: the energy supplied is used to break the bonds / overcome the forces between the particles
rather than to increase the kinetic energy of the particles

parts.examinerComment: Answers that said 'the heat is used up' were too vague to gain credit.

questions.stem: This question is about thermal energy transfer.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: A vacuum flask has double glass walls with a vacuum between them. The walls are silvered and the flask has a plastic stopper. Explain how the flask reduces thermal energy transfer. Refer to conduction, convection and radiation.

markingPoints.text: the vacuum prevents conduction (and convection) because there are no particles
the silvered surfaces reflect infrared radiation / are poor emitters
the stopper reduces convection (and evaporation) from the top
the plastic stopper is a poor conductor

parts.examinerComment: Candidates who matched each feature to the process it reduces scored well.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Explain why a thick woollen jumper keeps you warm.

markingPoints.text: wool traps air
air is a poor thermal conductor / an insulator
the trapped air cannot move, so convection is reduced

parts.examinerComment: Wool does not 'give out heat'; it reduces the rate of energy loss.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Describe an experiment to compare how well a matt black surface and a shiny silver surface emit infrared radiation.

markingPoints.text: use two identical containers, one painted matt black and one shiny silver
fill both with the same volume of hot water at the same starting temperature
measure the temperature of each after the same time (with a thermometer)
the one that cools faster (matt black) is the better emitter

parts.examinerComment: Answers needed to show a fair test with at least two controlled variables.

questions.stem: A student uses a ripple tank to study water waves.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: A student counts {n} waves passing a point in {t} s. Calculate the frequency of the waves, in Hz.

markingPoints.text: C1 for frequency = number of waves ÷ time
A1 for {=round(n/t,3)} Hz

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Waves of frequency {f} Hz have a wavelength of {lam} cm. Calculate the speed of the waves, in cm/s.

markingPoints.text: C1 for v = fλ
A1 for {=f*lam} cm/s

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: State the difference between a transverse wave and a longitudinal wave.

markingPoints.text: in a transverse wave the vibrations are perpendicular to the direction of travel (energy transfer)
in a longitudinal wave the vibrations are parallel to the direction of travel

parts.examinerComment: Some candidates gave examples without explaining the difference.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: The waves pass from deep water into shallower water. State what happens to their speed and to their wavelength.

markingPoints.text: the speed decreases
the wavelength decreases

parts.examinerComment: The frequency stays the same because it is set by the source.

questions.stem: This question is about light.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: State what is meant by the normal, and describe how the ray changes direction as it enters the glass.

markingPoints.text: the normal is a line at 90° to the surface at the point where the ray meets it
the ray bends towards the normal

parts.examinerComment: Angles of incidence and refraction are measured from the normal, not from the surface.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A ray of light strikes a plane mirror. The angle between the ray and the surface of the mirror is {a}°. Calculate the angle of reflection, in degrees.

markingPoints.text: C1 for angle of incidence = 90° − {a}° = {=90-a}°
A1 for angle of reflection = {=90-a}°

parts.examinerComment: The most common error was to give {a}°, forgetting that angles are measured from the normal.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Describe what is meant by total internal reflection. Give one example of where it is used.

markingPoints.text: light travels in a denser medium (e.g. glass) towards a boundary with a less dense medium (e.g. air)
the angle of incidence is greater than the critical angle
all the light is reflected back into the denser medium
example: optical fibres / prisms in periscopes or binoculars / cat's eyes (road reflectors)

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers referred to the critical angle.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: An object is placed further than two focal lengths from a converging lens. Describe the image formed.

markingPoints.text: real
inverted
diminished (smaller than the object)
formed between F and 2F on the other side of the lens

parts.examinerComment: Many candidates described the image formed by a magnifying glass instead.

questions.stem: This question is about the electromagnetic spectrum.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Name the region of the electromagnetic spectrum used for (i) television remote controls, (ii) producing images of broken bones.

markingPoints.text: (i) infrared
(ii) X-rays

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: State one harmful effect on people of excessive exposure to (i) ultraviolet radiation, (ii) microwaves.

markingPoints.text: (i) damage to surface cells and eyes / skin cancer / eye conditions
(ii) internal heating of body cells

parts.examinerComment: General answers such as 'it is dangerous' did not gain credit.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Name the region of the electromagnetic spectrum between visible light and X-rays.

markingPoints.text: ultraviolet

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: State two properties shared by all electromagnetic waves.

markingPoints.text: they are transverse waves
they all travel at the same speed in a vacuum
they can travel through a vacuum
they transfer energy

parts.examinerComment: Any two correct properties gained the marks.

questions.stem: This question is about sound.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Describe a method to measure the speed of sound in air outdoors, using two wooden blocks, a stopwatch and a measuring tape.

markingPoints.text: measure a large distance (e.g. over 100 m) between two people with the tape
one person bangs the blocks together, making a sound and a visible action
the other starts the stopwatch on seeing the blocks hit and stops it on hearing the sound
speed = distance ÷ time
repeat several times and calculate an average time

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers explained that a large distance makes the time long compared with reaction time.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: In such an experiment, two students stand {=v*t} m apart. The average time measured is {t} s. Calculate the speed of sound, in m/s.

markingPoints.text: C1 for speed = distance ÷ time
A1 for {v} m/s

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: A guitar string is plucked. Describe how the sound reaches a listener's ear.

markingPoints.text: the vibrating string makes the air particles next to it vibrate
the vibrations are passed through the air as a longitudinal wave (compressions and rarefactions) to the ear

parts.examinerComment: Sound is a vibration passed from particle to particle; air does not flow from the guitar to the ear.

questions.stem: This question is about magnets.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Describe the difference between a temporary magnet and a permanent magnet. Name a material used for each.

markingPoints.text: a temporary (induced) magnet loses its magnetism when removed from the magnetic field
a permanent magnet keeps its magnetism
temporary: soft iron
permanent: steel

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers named a suitable material for each type.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Describe the pattern and direction of the magnetic field around a bar magnet.

markingPoints.text: field lines go from the north pole to the south pole outside the magnet
the lines are closest together at the poles (strongest field)
the lines do not cross
the pattern is symmetrical / lines spread out further from the magnet

parts.examinerComment: Arrows on field lines must point away from the north pole.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: State what happens when the north pole of one magnet is brought near the south pole of another magnet.

markingPoints.text: they attract

parts.examinerComment: Like poles repel; unlike poles attract.

questions.stem: A student investigates the resistance of a filament lamp.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Describe how the student connects an ammeter and a voltmeter to measure the current in the lamp and the potential difference across it.

markingPoints.text: the ammeter is connected in series with the lamp
the voltmeter is connected in parallel with (across) the lamp

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: The voltmeter reads {Vv} V and the ammeter reads {I} A. Calculate the resistance of the lamp, in Ω.

markingPoints.text: C1 for R = V ÷ I
A1 for {=round(Vv/I,2)} Ω

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: State how the resistance of a metal wire changes if (i) a longer wire of the same thickness is used, (ii) a thicker wire of the same length is used.

markingPoints.text: (i) the resistance increases
(ii) the resistance decreases

parts.examinerComment: Some candidates thought a thicker wire has a greater resistance.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Explain the difference between direct current (d.c.) and alternating current (a.c.).

markingPoints.text: direct current flows in one direction only
alternating current repeatedly changes direction

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

questions.stem: This question is about series and parallel circuits.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: A {R1} Ω resistor and a {R2} Ω resistor are connected in series with a {Vs} V battery. Calculate the current in the circuit, in A.

markingPoints.text: C1 for total resistance = {R1} + {R2} = {=R1+R2} Ω
C1 for I = V ÷ R
A1 for {=round(Vs/(R1+R2),3)} A

parts.examinerComment: Using only one of the resistors was a common error.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Two identical lamps are connected in parallel to a cell. State how the current from the cell compares with the current in each lamp.

markingPoints.text: the current from the cell is larger than the current in each lamp
it is the sum of the two lamp currents / twice the current in one lamp

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers stated that the current splits between the branches.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Give two advantages of connecting the lamps in a house lighting circuit in parallel rather than in series.

markingPoints.text: each lamp has the full supply voltage across it (so stays bright)
each lamp can be switched on and off independently
if one lamp fails, the others stay on

parts.examinerComment: Any two advantages gained the marks.

questions.stem: A toaster with a metal case is connected to the mains supply with a three-core cable.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Name the three wires in the cable.

markingPoints.text: live
neutral and earth (both needed)

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: State and explain one hazard of plugging too many appliances into one socket.

markingPoints.text: the current in the cable or socket is too large
the cable overheats, which could cause a fire

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers linked the large current to overheating.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: A hairdryer has a plastic case and is double insulated. Explain why it does not need an earth wire.

markingPoints.text: the case is an insulator, so it cannot become live
there are no exposed metal parts that a user could touch

parts.examinerComment: Most candidates knew plastic is an insulator.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Explain how a fuse protects the toaster and its cable.

markingPoints.text: if the current becomes larger than the fuse rating, the fuse wire melts
this breaks the circuit, stopping the current before the cable overheats

parts.examinerComment: A fuse does not 'reduce' the current; it stops it completely.

questions.stem: This question is about electromagnetic effects.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: A coil is connected to a sensitive centre-zero meter. Describe what is seen on the meter when a magnet is pushed into the coil, held still inside it, and then pulled out.

markingPoints.text: pushed in: the needle deflects (an e.m.f. is induced)
held still: no deflection / reading is zero
pulled out: the needle deflects in the opposite direction

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers recognised that an e.m.f. is only induced when the magnetic field through the coil is changing.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Describe the magnetic field pattern around a long straight wire carrying a current.

markingPoints.text: circles centred on the wire (in a plane perpendicular to the wire)
the circles are further apart further from the wire / the field is weaker further away

parts.examinerComment: Some candidates drew the pattern for a bar magnet.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: A step-up transformer has {Np} turns on its primary coil and {=Np*k} turns on its secondary coil. The input voltage is {Vp} V. Calculate the output voltage, in V.

markingPoints.text: C1 for Vs ÷ Vp = Ns ÷ Np
A1 for {=Vp*k} V

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Explain why electricity is transmitted across the country at very high voltages.

markingPoints.text: for the same power, a high voltage means a small current
so less energy is wasted as heat in the cables (and thinner, cheaper cables can be used)

parts.examinerComment: Answers needed to link high voltage to low current.

questions.stem: This question is about the structure of the atom.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Describe the structure of an atom. State where the protons, neutrons and electrons are found.

markingPoints.text: a small central nucleus
containing protons and neutrons
electrons orbit the nucleus / are found outside the nucleus
the nucleus is very small compared with the size of the atom

parts.examinerComment: Some candidates placed electrons in the nucleus.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A neutral atom has a nucleon number of {=2*Z+d} and a proton number of {Z}. State the number of electrons in the atom.

markingPoints.text: B1 for {Z}

parts.examinerComment: In a neutral atom the number of electrons equals the number of protons.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Explain how an atom becomes a positive ion.

markingPoints.text: the atom loses one or more electrons
so it has more protons than electrons

parts.examinerComment: An atom cannot gain protons to become an ion.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Describe the difference between nuclear fission and nuclear fusion.

markingPoints.text: fission: a large nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei
fusion: two light nuclei join to form a heavier nucleus
both release energy

parts.examinerComment: Candidates often mixed up the two terms.

questions.stem: This question is about radioactivity.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Compare alpha, beta and gamma radiation in terms of their ionising effect and their penetrating ability.

markingPoints.text: alpha is the most ionising and the least penetrating (stopped by paper / a few cm of air)
beta is moderately ionising and penetrating (stopped by a few mm of aluminium)
gamma is the least ionising and the most penetrating (reduced by thick lead or concrete)

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers gave a suitable absorber for each type.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A sample contains {=k*2^n} mg of a radioactive isotope with a half-life of {T} years. Calculate the mass of the isotope remaining after {=n*T} years, in mg.

markingPoints.text: C1 for {n} half-lives
A1 for {k} mg

parts.examinerComment: Count the number of half-lives first, then halve that many times.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: State three precautions that should be taken when using a radioactive source in a school laboratory.

markingPoints.text: handle the source with tongs
keep the source as far from the body as possible / point it away from people
use it for as short a time as possible
store it in a lead-lined box when not in use
wash hands after the experiment

parts.examinerComment: Any three sensible precautions were accepted.

questions.stem: This question is about the Earth and the Solar System.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Explain why the Moon appears to change shape (show phases) during a month.

markingPoints.text: the Moon reflects light from the Sun (it does not produce its own light)
as the Moon orbits the Earth, we see different amounts of its sunlit half

parts.examinerComment: The phases are not caused by the Earth's shadow; that is an eclipse.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Mars is {d} × 10¹¹ m from the Sun. Light travels at 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. Calculate the time taken for light from the Sun to reach Mars, in s.

markingPoints.text: C1 for time = distance ÷ speed
A1 for {=round(d*1000/3,1)} s

parts.examinerComment: Standard form caused difficulties for some candidates. The answer can be typed as, for example, 767 or 7.67e2.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Name the force that keeps the planets in orbit around the Sun, and state where most of the mass of the Solar System is.

markingPoints.text: gravity / gravitational attraction (of the Sun)
in the Sun

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: State two differences between the four inner planets and the four outer planets.

markingPoints.text: the inner planets are rocky; the outer planets are gaseous (gas giants)
the inner planets are smaller; the outer planets are larger
the outer planets are colder / take longer to orbit the Sun

parts.examinerComment: Any two correct differences gained the marks.

questions.stem: This question is about stars and the Universe.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: State what is meant by a light-year, and explain why it is used for distances in astronomy.

markingPoints.text: the distance travelled by light in (space in) one year
astronomical distances are so large that metres would give very large numbers

parts.examinerComment: A light-year is a distance, not a time.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A star is {n} light-years from the Earth. 1 light-year = 9.5 × 10¹⁵ m. Calculate the distance to the star, in m.

markingPoints.text: C1 for {n} × 9.5 × 10¹⁵
A1 for {=round(n*0.95,4)} × 10¹⁶ m

parts.examinerComment: Answers in standard form can be typed as, for example, 8.2e16.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Describe what is meant by redshift and explain how it provides evidence for the Big Bang theory.

markingPoints.text: light from distant galaxies has a longer wavelength than expected / is shifted towards the red end of the spectrum
this shows that the galaxies are moving away from us
so the Universe is expanding
which suggests it started from a single, very small point (the Big Bang)

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers linked each step of the argument.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Name the galaxy that contains the Sun, and state roughly how many stars a galaxy contains.

markingPoints.text: the Milky Way
many billions of stars

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: A boat heads due north at {v} m/s relative to the water. A current carries the water due east at {u} m/s. Calculate the magnitude of the boat's resultant velocity, in m/s.

markingPoints.text: C1 for √({v}² + {u}²)
A1 for {=round(sqrt(v^2+u^2),2)} m/s

parts.examinerComment: The velocities are at right angles, so they cannot simply be added. A scale drawing was also accepted.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A boat heads due north at {v} m/s relative to the water, in a current flowing due east at {u} m/s. Calculate the angle between the boat's resultant velocity and due north, in degrees.

markingPoints.text: C1 for tan θ = {u} ÷ {v}
A1 for {=round(atan(u/v)*180/pi,1)}°

parts.examinerComment: Some candidates found the angle from due east instead. A sketch of the vector triangle helps to identify the correct angle.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Explain the difference between a scalar quantity and a vector quantity. Give one example of each, other than velocity and speed.

markingPoints.text: a scalar has magnitude (size) only
a vector has both magnitude and direction
a correct scalar example, e.g. mass, distance, energy, time, temperature
a correct vector example, e.g. force, weight, acceleration, momentum, displacement

parts.examinerComment: Weight was sometimes wrongly given as a scalar; it is a force and so has a direction.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: A car travels around a roundabout at a constant speed of 8 m/s. A student says the car has a constant velocity. Explain why the student is wrong.

markingPoints.text: velocity is a vector / velocity includes direction
the direction of motion keeps changing, so the velocity changes (even though the speed does not)

parts.examinerComment: Candidates who stated that velocity is speed in a given direction usually gained both marks.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: A skydiver jumps from a hovering helicopter. Explain, in terms of the forces acting, why the skydiver reaches a terminal velocity.

markingPoints.text: weight acts downwards and stays constant
air resistance increases as the speed increases
so the resultant force and the acceleration decrease
at terminal velocity air resistance equals weight, the resultant force is zero and the speed is constant

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers named both forces and linked a zero resultant force to zero acceleration, not to zero speed.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: When the parachute opens, the skydiver slows from {u} m/s to {v} m/s in {t} s. Calculate the average deceleration, in m/s².

markingPoints.text: C1 for a = (u − v) ÷ t
A1 for {=round((u-v)/t,3)} m/s²

parts.examinerComment: Some candidates divided the final speed by the time, ignoring the initial speed.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: A car accelerates uniformly from {u} m/s to {v} m/s in {t} s. Calculate the distance travelled during this time, in m.

markingPoints.text: C1 for distance = area under the speed–time graph
C1 for ½ × ({u} + {v}) × {t}
A1 for {=(u+v)/2*t} m

parts.examinerComment: The area is a trapezium (or a rectangle plus a triangle). Using only the final speed overestimates the distance.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Explain why the gravitational field strength g is equal to the acceleration of free fall.

markingPoints.text: g = W ÷ m, the force per unit mass
a = F ÷ m, and for an object falling freely the only force is its weight
so a = W ÷ m = g (for all masses, if there is no air resistance)

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers used F = ma with the weight as the resultant force.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A space probe of mass {m} kg has a weight of {=round(m*g,2)} N on the surface of a planet. Calculate the gravitational field strength at the planet's surface, in N/kg.

markingPoints.text: C1 for g = W ÷ m
A1 for {=round(round(m*g,2)/m,3)} N/kg

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: On a planet where g = {g} N/kg, a stone is dropped from rest. Ignoring air resistance, calculate its speed after {t} s, in m/s.

markingPoints.text: C1 for acceleration = g = {g} m/s²
A1 for v = {g} × {t} = {=g*t} m/s

parts.examinerComment: The acceleration of free fall is numerically equal to g on that planet.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: A metal rod has length {L} cm and a uniform cross-sectional area of {A} cm². Its mass is {=round(rho*L*A,1)} g. Calculate the density of the metal, in kg/m³.

markingPoints.text: C1 for volume = {=L*A} cm³
C1 for density = {=round(round(rho*L*A,1)/(L*A),3)} g/cm³
A1 for {=round(round(rho*L*A,1)/(L*A)*1000,1)} kg/m³ (1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³)

parts.examinerComment: Unit conversion caused difficulty. 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³; it is not 100 or 1 000 000.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A solid plastic ball has a density of 1.02 g/cm³. Fresh water has a density of 1.00 g/cm³ and sea water has a density of 1.03 g/cm³. Predict and explain what happens when the ball is placed in each liquid.

markingPoints.text: it sinks in fresh water
because its density is greater than that of fresh water
it floats in sea water
because its density is less than that of sea water

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers compared densities in each case rather than referring to the 'weight' or 'heaviness' of the ball.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: A room measures {a} m × {b} m × {h} m. The density of air is 1.2 kg/m³. Calculate the mass of air in the room, in kg.

markingPoints.text: C1 for volume = {a} × {b} × {h}
A1 for m = ρV = {=round(1.2*a*b*h,3)} kg

parts.examinerComment: Many candidates were surprised by the size of the answer, but the result is correct: air has a significant mass.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: A spring obeys Hooke's law. A load of {F} N produces an extension of {x} cm. Calculate the spring constant, in N/m.

markingPoints.text: C1 for x = {=x/100} m
C1 for k = F ÷ x
A1 for {=round(F/(x/100),2)} N/m

parts.examinerComment: Many candidates did not convert centimetres to metres.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A car of mass {m} kg has a driving force of {Fd} N. The total resistive force on it is {Fr} N. Calculate the acceleration of the car, in m/s².

markingPoints.text: C1 for resultant force = {Fd} − {Fr} = {=Fd-Fr} N
C1 for a = F ÷ m
A1 for {=round((Fd-Fr)/m,3)} m/s²

parts.examinerComment: The acceleration is produced by the resultant force, not by the driving force alone.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: State the two conditions needed for an object to be in equilibrium.

markingPoints.text: there is no resultant force
there is no resultant moment / clockwise moments equal anticlockwise moments

parts.examinerComment: Both conditions are needed: balanced forces alone do not stop an object turning.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: A ball on a string is whirled in a horizontal circle at constant speed. State and explain how the tension in the string must change if (i) the speed increases with the radius unchanged, (ii) the radius increases with the speed unchanged.

markingPoints.text: the tension provides the force towards the centre of the circle
(i) the tension must increase
(ii) the tension can decrease / a smaller force is needed for a larger radius

parts.examinerComment: Weaker answers described an outward force. The resultant force in circular motion always acts towards the centre.

questions.stem: This question is about momentum and impulse.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: A cannon of mass {M} kg is at rest. It fires a shell of mass {m} kg horizontally at {v} m/s. Calculate the recoil speed of the cannon, in m/s.

markingPoints.text: C1 for total momentum before firing = 0
C1 for {M} × V = {m} × {v}
A1 for {=round(m*v/M,3)} m/s

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers stated that the total momentum is zero before and after, so the two momenta are equal and opposite.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A footballer kicks a stationary ball of mass {m} kg. The foot is in contact with the ball for {t} s and the ball leaves the foot at {v} m/s. Calculate the average force on the ball, in N.

markingPoints.text: C1 for change in momentum = {m} × {v} = {=round(m*v,4)} kg m/s
C1 for F = Δp ÷ Δt
A1 for {=round(m*v/t,2)} N

parts.examinerComment: Resultant force = rate of change of momentum. Several candidates multiplied by the time instead of dividing.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Explain, using ideas about momentum, why the crumple zone of a car reduces the force on the passengers in a collision.

markingPoints.text: the change in momentum of the passengers is the same (they are brought to rest from the same speed)
the crumple zone increases the time taken for the car to stop
force = change in momentum ÷ time, so the force is smaller

parts.examinerComment: Answers that only said the crumple zone 'absorbs the force' gained no credit.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Trolley A, of mass {mA} kg, moves to the right at {uA} m/s. It collides with trolley B, of mass {mB} kg, which is moving to the left at {uB} m/s. The trolleys stick together. Calculate their velocity after the collision, in m/s, taking right as positive.

markingPoints.text: C1 for total momentum before = {mA} × {uA} − {mB} × {uB} = {=mA*uA-mB*uB} kg m/s
C1 for dividing by the total mass {=mA+mB} kg
A1 for {=round((mA*uA-mB*uB)/(mA+mB),3)} m/s (to the right)

parts.examinerComment: Many candidates added the two momenta. Momentum to the left must be given a negative sign.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: A ball of mass {m} kg is dropped from rest from a height of {h} m. Ignoring air resistance, calculate its speed just before it hits the ground, in m/s. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

markingPoints.text: C1 for loss of gravitational potential energy = mgh = {=round(m*9.8*h,3)} J
C1 for ½mv² = mgh
A1 for v = {=round(sqrt(19.6*h),2)} m/s

parts.examinerComment: The mass cancels, but candidates who calculated the energy first and then used it were equally successful.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: An electric motor is supplied with {=round(m*9.8*h*100/e)} J of energy. It lifts a mass of {m} kg through a height of {h} m. Calculate the efficiency of the motor, as a percentage. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

markingPoints.text: C1 for useful energy output = mgh = {=round(m*9.8*h,3)} J
C1 for efficiency = useful output ÷ total input × 100%

parts.examinerComment: Some candidates divided the input by the output, giving an efficiency over 100%. Always check the answer is sensible.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Describe how electricity is generated in a hydroelectric power station. Name the energy stores involved.

markingPoints.text: water is stored at a height behind a dam (gravitational potential store)
water flows downhill, gaining kinetic energy
the moving water turns a turbine
the turbine drives a generator, which transfers the energy electrically

parts.examinerComment: Most candidates knew the sequence; the best answers named the energy stores at each stage.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: A car of mass {m} kg is travelling at {v} m/s. The brakes bring it to rest in a distance of {d} m. Calculate the average braking force, in N.

markingPoints.text: C1 for kinetic energy = ½mv² = {=0.5*m*v^2} J
C1 for work done by brakes = force × distance = kinetic energy
A1 for {=round(0.5*m*v^2/d,1)} N

parts.examinerComment: A good answer links work done to the energy transferred out of the kinetic store.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: A swimming pool is {h} m deep. Atmospheric pressure is {pa} Pa. Calculate the total pressure on the bottom of the pool, in Pa. (density of water = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.8 N/kg)

markingPoints.text: C1 for pressure due to water = ρgh = {=round(1000*9.8*h,1)} Pa
C1 for adding atmospheric pressure
A1 for {=round(pa+1000*9.8*h,1)} Pa

parts.examinerComment: Many candidates forgot that the atmosphere also presses on the water surface.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A window in a submarine has an area of {A} m². Calculate the force on the window from the water when the submarine is {d} m below the surface of the sea. Ignore atmospheric pressure. (density of sea water = 1030 kg/m³, g = 9.8 N/kg)

markingPoints.text: C1 for p = ρgh = {=round(1030*9.8*d,1)} Pa
C1 for F = pA
A1 for {=round(1030*9.8*d*A,1)} N

parts.examinerComment: Candidates who calculated the pressure first and then the force rarely made errors.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Explain why the pressure 10 m below the surface of the sea is greater than the pressure 10 m below the surface of a freshwater lake.

markingPoints.text: sea water has a greater density than fresh water
pressure = ρgh, so at the same depth a denser liquid gives a greater pressure

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: A bubble of gas has a volume of {V1} cm³ at a pressure of {p1} kPa at the bottom of a lake. It rises to the surface, where the pressure is {p2} kPa. The temperature stays constant. Calculate the volume of the bubble at the surface, in cm³.

markingPoints.text: C1 for p₁V₁ = p₂V₂
A1 for {=round(p1*V1/p2,3)} cm³

parts.examinerComment: The bubble expands as the pressure falls. Candidates who obtained a smaller volume should have checked their answer.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Explain, in terms of the momentum of the particles, how a gas exerts a pressure on the walls of its container, and why the pressure increases when the gas is heated at constant volume.

markingPoints.text: a particle hitting a wall rebounds, so its momentum changes
the wall exerts a force on the particle, so the particle exerts a force on the wall (force = rate of change of momentum)
pressure is the total force per unit area of wall
when heated the particles move faster, so each collision gives a larger change in momentum
and there are more collisions per second

parts.examinerComment: Few candidates referred to momentum. Stronger answers identified two reasons for the increase: harder and more frequent collisions.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: State the temperature of absolute zero, in °C.

markingPoints.text: B1 for −273 °C

parts.examinerComment: At absolute zero the particles have the least possible kinetic energy.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: An electric heater of power {P} W heats a {m} kg aluminium block for {t} s. The temperature of the block rises by {=round(P*t/(m*c),1)} °C. Assuming no energy is lost, calculate the specific heat capacity of aluminium, in J/(kg °C).

markingPoints.text: C1 for energy supplied = Pt = {=P*t} J
C1 for c = ΔE ÷ (mΔθ)
A1 for {=round(P*t/(m*round(P*t/(m*c),1)),1)} J/(kg °C)

parts.examinerComment: Candidates who calculated the energy first were more successful. In practice some energy is lost, so the measured value is too high.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: State two differences between boiling and evaporation.

markingPoints.text: boiling happens at one fixed temperature (the boiling point); evaporation happens at any temperature
boiling happens throughout the liquid (bubbles form); evaporation happens only at the surface

parts.examinerComment: Each difference needed both processes to be described.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Wet clothes dry more quickly on a warm, windy day. Explain why, in terms of particles.

markingPoints.text: at a higher temperature more particles have enough energy to escape from the surface
the wind removes the water vapour molecules from near the surface
so fewer molecules return to the liquid
spreading clothes out increases the surface area from which particles can escape

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers explained both factors given in the question.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Explain, in terms of particles, why a metal bar expands when it is heated.

markingPoints.text: the particles gain kinetic energy and vibrate with a larger amplitude
so the average separation of the particles increases

parts.examinerComment: The particles do not expand; they move further apart.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Explain, in terms of particles, how thermal energy is conducted along a metal rod.

markingPoints.text: atoms (ions) at the hot end vibrate with more energy
they pass energy to neighbouring atoms through the lattice
free electrons gain kinetic energy and move quickly through the metal
they transfer energy by colliding with atoms further along the rod

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers described both mechanisms and stated that the electron mechanism is faster.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: State how the rate at which an object emits infrared radiation depends on (i) its surface temperature, (ii) its surface area.

markingPoints.text: (i) the higher the temperature, the greater the rate of emission
(ii) the larger the surface area, the greater the rate of emission

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Explain how the temperature of the Earth depends on the balance between the radiation it receives and the radiation it emits.

markingPoints.text: the Earth absorbs radiation (mainly visible light and infrared) from the Sun
the Earth emits infrared radiation into space
if the rates are equal, the average temperature stays constant
if less radiation is emitted than absorbed (e.g. more greenhouse gases), the temperature rises

parts.examinerComment: Some candidates confused this with the ozone layer, which absorbs ultraviolet radiation.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Explain why convection cannot take place in a solid.

markingPoints.text: convection needs the bulk movement of a fluid (liquid or gas) / currents
particles in a solid are held in fixed positions and cannot flow

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: A radio station broadcasts at a frequency of {f} MHz. Radio waves travel at 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. Calculate the wavelength of the waves, in m.

markingPoints.text: C1 for λ = v ÷ f with f = {f} × 10⁶ Hz
A1 for {=round(300/f,3)} m

parts.examinerComment: Candidates who forgot that 1 MHz = 10⁶ Hz gave very large wavelengths.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Describe how a ripple tank is used to show the refraction of water waves, and state what is observed.

markingPoints.text: place a glass (or plastic) sheet in the tank to make a region of shallow water
waves travel more slowly in the shallow water
the wavefronts are closer together (shorter wavelength) in the shallow water
if the boundary is at an angle, the waves change direction

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers explained that refraction is caused by the change in speed.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: A house is in a valley behind a hill. Explain why it can receive long-wave radio signals from a distant transmitter but not signals of much shorter wavelength.

markingPoints.text: long-wavelength waves diffract (spread) around the hill
diffraction is greatest when the wavelength is similar to the size of the obstacle; short wavelengths diffract very little

parts.examinerComment: Many candidates used the word 'diffract' correctly but did not link it to wavelength.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: A wave travels {=v*t} m in {t} s. Its wavelength is {lam} m. Calculate its frequency, in Hz.

markingPoints.text: C1 for speed = {=v*t} ÷ {t} = {v} m/s
A1 for f = v ÷ λ = {=round(v/lam,3)} Hz

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Light travels at 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s in air and at {v} × 10⁸ m/s in a transparent plastic. Calculate the refractive index of the plastic.

markingPoints.text: C1 for n = speed in air ÷ speed in plastic
A1 for {=round(3/v,3)}

parts.examinerComment: A refractive index has no unit and is always greater than 1.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A ray of light enters a glass block of refractive index {n} with an angle of incidence of {i}°. Calculate the angle of refraction, in degrees.

markingPoints.text: C1 for n = sin i ÷ sin r
C1 for sin r = sin {i}° ÷ {n} = {=round(sin(i*pi/180)/n,4)}
A1 for r = {=round(asin(sin(i*pi/180)/n)*180/pi,1)}°

parts.examinerComment: The angle of refraction must be smaller than the angle of incidence when light enters glass.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Describe how an optical fibre transmits light, and give one use of optical fibres in telecommunications or medicine.

markingPoints.text: light hits the inside surface of the fibre at an angle greater than the critical angle
it is totally internally reflected
this happens repeatedly along the fibre, even when it bends
use: carrying telephone / internet data, or in an endoscope to see inside the body

parts.examinerComment: Weaker answers said the light is 'refracted along the fibre'.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Explain how a converging lens is used as a magnifying glass. Describe the image formed.

markingPoints.text: the object is placed closer to the lens than the principal focus (less than one focal length)
the image is virtual
upright and enlarged
on the same side of the lens as the object

parts.examinerComment: Many candidates knew the image is enlarged but forgot that it is virtual.

parts.label: (e)
parts.prompt: State the type of lens used to correct short-sightedness and explain how it works.

markingPoints.text: a diverging lens
a short-sighted eye focuses light from distant objects in front of the retina; the lens spreads the rays so they focus on the retina

parts.examinerComment: Converging lenses correct long-sightedness.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: X-rays used in a hospital have a frequency of {f} × 10¹⁸ Hz. Calculate their wavelength, in m. (speed of electromagnetic waves = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s)

markingPoints.text: C1 for λ = v ÷ f
A1 for {=round(3/f,3)} × 10⁻¹⁰ m

parts.examinerComment: Answers in standard form can be typed as, for example, 1.0e-10.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Explain the difference between analogue and digital signals, and give two advantages of transmitting sound as a digital signal.

markingPoints.text: an analogue signal varies continuously
a digital signal has only two values (on/off, 1/0)
digital signals can be regenerated, removing noise, so they travel long distances without loss of quality
digital signals allow a higher rate of data transmission

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers explained why noise can be removed from a digital signal.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Explain why radiographers who take X-ray images stand behind a lead screen.

markingPoints.text: X-rays are ionising and can damage cells / cause mutations or cancer
lead absorbs X-rays, and radiographers would otherwise receive repeated doses

parts.examinerComment: Answers needed to explain why repeated exposure matters for workers.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Describe a sound wave in air in terms of compressions and rarefactions.

markingPoints.text: sound is a longitudinal wave; air particles vibrate parallel to the direction of travel
compressions are regions where the particles are close together (higher pressure)
rarefactions are regions where the particles are further apart (lower pressure)

parts.examinerComment: Well answered by most candidates.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A note has a frequency of {f} Hz. Sound travels in air at {v} m/s. Calculate the wavelength of the note, in m.

markingPoints.text: C1 for λ = v ÷ f
A1 for {=round(v/f,4)} m

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Describe one medical use of ultrasound and explain why it is suitable for this use.

markingPoints.text: e.g. scanning a fetus / imaging soft tissues inside the body
ultrasound is partly reflected at boundaries between tissues; the echoes are used to build an image
it is not ionising, so it is safe for the fetus / patient

parts.examinerComment: Answers that described X-ray imaging gained no credit.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: An ultrasound pulse is reflected from a boundary inside the body. The echo returns {t} × 10⁻⁵ s after the pulse is sent. The speed of ultrasound in soft tissue is 1500 m/s. Calculate the depth of the boundary below the skin, in cm.

markingPoints.text: C1 for distance travelled = 1500 × {t} × 10⁻⁵ m
C1 for dividing by 2 (there and back)
A1 for {=round(0.75*t,3)} cm

parts.examinerComment: Common errors were forgetting to halve the distance and not converting to centimetres.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Explain why the core of an electromagnet used in a relay is made of soft iron rather than steel.

markingPoints.text: soft iron is easily magnetised (so the field is strong when the current flows)
soft iron loses its magnetism when the current is switched off; steel would stay magnetised

parts.examinerComment: Most candidates knew soft iron is a temporary magnet.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Give two uses of permanent magnets and two uses of electromagnets.

markingPoints.text: permanent magnet use, e.g. compass, loudspeaker
a second permanent magnet use, e.g. electric motor, fridge door seal, microphone
electromagnet use, e.g. scrapyard crane, relay
a second electromagnet use, e.g. electric bell, MRI scanner, circuit breaker

parts.examinerComment: Electromagnets are used where the magnetism must be switched on and off.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Describe how a plotting compass is used to find the direction of the magnetic field at a point near a bar magnet.

markingPoints.text: place the plotting compass at the point
the north end of the needle points in the direction of the field

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: A magnet can pick up a chain of iron paper clips, each clip hanging from the one above. Explain how this happens.

markingPoints.text: the first clip is in the magnet's field and becomes an induced magnet
the pole induced nearest the magnet is opposite to the magnet's pole, so it is attracted
the first clip then induces magnetism in the next clip, and so on

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers used the term induced magnetism.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: An electric kettle of power {P} W is switched on for {t} minutes. Calculate the energy transferred, in J.

markingPoints.text: C1 for E = Pt with t = {=t*60} s
A1 for {=P*t*60} J

parts.examinerComment: Minutes must be converted to seconds.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A lamp is connected to a {Vv} V supply and the current in it is {I} A. Calculate the power of the lamp, in W.

markingPoints.text: C1 for P = IV
A1 for {=Vv*I} W

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: A metal wire of length {L} m has a resistance of {R} Ω. Calculate the resistance of a wire of the same metal that is {L2} m long and has twice the cross-sectional area, in Ω.

markingPoints.text: C1 for resistance is proportional to length: × {=round(L2/L,4)}
C1 for resistance is inversely proportional to area: ÷ 2
A1 for {=round(R*(L2/L)/2,3)} Ω

parts.examinerComment: Candidates often dealt with only one of the two changes.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: An electric heater of power {P} kW is used for {h} hours each day for {d} days. Electricity costs {c} cents per kW h. Calculate the total cost of using the heater, in cents.

markingPoints.text: C1 for energy = power × time in kW h
C1 for {P} × {h} × {d} = {=P*h*d} kW h
A1 for {=P*h*d*c} cents

parts.examinerComment: Power in kW and time in hours give energy in kW h directly.

parts.label: (e)
parts.prompt: Describe the shape of the current–voltage graph for a filament lamp and explain the shape.

markingPoints.text: the graph is a curve through the origin
the gradient decreases as the voltage increases / current increases less than proportionally
the filament gets hotter as the current increases
so its resistance increases

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers linked the change in resistance to the temperature of the filament.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: A {R1} Ω resistor is connected in series with two {R2} Ω resistors that are connected in parallel with each other. The combination is connected to a {Vs} V supply. Calculate the current from the supply, in A.

markingPoints.text: C1 for parallel pair = {=R2/2} Ω
C1 for total resistance = {=R1+R2/2} Ω
A1 for I = {=round(Vs/(R1+R2/2),3)} A

parts.examinerComment: Work out the parallel combination first, then add the series resistor.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A thermistor and a fixed resistor are connected in series as a potential divider across a battery. Explain what happens to the potential difference across the fixed resistor when the temperature of the thermistor rises.

markingPoints.text: the resistance of the thermistor decreases as its temperature rises
the thermistor takes a smaller share of the supply p.d.
so the p.d. across the fixed resistor increases

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers explained the change in terms of the share of the p.d.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: A {Vs} V battery is connected across a {R1} Ω resistor and a {R2} Ω resistor that are connected in parallel. Calculate the current from the battery, in A.

markingPoints.text: C1 for current in each branch: {Vs} ÷ {R1} and {Vs} ÷ {R2}
C1 for adding the branch currents (or using the combined resistance)
A1 for {=round(Vs/R1+Vs/R2,3)} A

parts.examinerComment: The full supply p.d. is across each branch of a parallel circuit.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: An appliance with a power of {P} W is connected to the 230 V mains supply. Calculate the current in the appliance, in A.

markingPoints.text: C1 for I = P ÷ V
A1 for {=round(P/230,3)} A

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A fault causes the live wire to touch the metal case of an earthed washing machine. Explain how the earth wire and the fuse together make the appliance safe.

markingPoints.text: a large current flows from the live wire through the case to earth
because the earth wire is a low-resistance path
the current is greater than the fuse rating, so the fuse melts
this disconnects the live wire, so the case is no longer live / cannot give a shock

parts.examinerComment: Many candidates thought the earth wire 'absorbs' the current. It provides a low-resistance path so that the fuse melts.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Explain why the switch on an appliance must be connected in the live wire and not in the neutral wire.

markingPoints.text: if the switch were in the neutral wire, the appliance would still be connected to the live wire when switched off
parts inside would still be at a high voltage, so a person could get a shock

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers referred to the high voltage of the live wire.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: State two advantages of a circuit breaker compared with a fuse.

markingPoints.text: it can be reset (does not need replacing)
it acts more quickly

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: A power station delivers {P} MW at {Vt} kV through cables with a total resistance of {R} Ω. Calculate the power wasted in the cables, in kW.

markingPoints.text: C1 for I = P ÷ V = {=round(P*1000/Vt,3)} A
C1 for power loss = I²R

parts.examinerComment: Candidates who used P = V²/R with the transmission voltage obtained a huge, incorrect answer: that V is not the p.d. across the cables.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Explain how a transformer produces an alternating p.d. across its secondary coil.

markingPoints.text: the alternating current in the primary coil produces a changing magnetic field
the iron core carries this changing field through the secondary coil
the changing field induces an alternating e.m.f. in the secondary coil
a steady d.c. input would produce no output (except at switching on or off)

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers emphasised that the magnetic field must be changing.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: A transformer that is 100% efficient steps down 230 V to {Vs} V. The current in the secondary coil is {Is} A. Calculate the current in the primary coil, in A.

markingPoints.text: C1 for VpIp = VsIs
A1 for {=round(Vs*Is/230,4)} A

parts.examinerComment: Power in = power out for a 100% efficient transformer, so the current is smaller on the high-voltage side.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Explain how the split-ring commutator keeps a d.c. motor turning in the same direction.

markingPoints.text: the commutator reverses the current in the coil
every half turn (when the coil is vertical)
so the forces on each side of the coil keep turning it in the same direction

parts.examinerComment: Many candidates knew that the commutator reverses the current but not when this happens.

parts.label: (e)
parts.prompt: A wire carrying a current is placed between the poles of a magnet and a force acts on it. State two changes that would reverse the direction of the force.

markingPoints.text: reverse the direction of the current
reverse the direction of the magnetic field (swap the poles)

parts.examinerComment: Reversing both at once leaves the force in the same direction.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: State the relative charge and relative mass of a proton, a neutron and an electron.

markingPoints.text: proton: charge +1, mass 1
neutron: charge 0, mass 1
electron: charge −1, mass about 1/2000 (negligible)

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: The charge on a proton is 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Calculate the charge on a nucleus with proton number {Z}, in C.

markingPoints.text: A1 for {=round(Z*0.16,3)} × 10⁻¹⁸ C

parts.examinerComment: Neutrons have no charge, so only the protons contribute.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Describe what happens when a uranium-235 nucleus undergoes fission in a nuclear reactor, and explain how a chain reaction occurs.

markingPoints.text: a neutron is absorbed by the uranium-235 nucleus
the nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei, releasing energy
two or three neutrons are also released
these neutrons can cause further fissions, giving a chain reaction

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers explained the role of the released neutrons.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Explain why two isotopes of the same element have different masses but the same proton number.

markingPoints.text: they have the same number of protons (that is what defines the element)
but different numbers of neutrons, so their masses differ

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Radioactive decay is described as random and spontaneous. Explain what these two words mean.

markingPoints.text: random: it is impossible to predict which nucleus will decay next or when
spontaneous: decay is not affected by external conditions such as temperature or pressure

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Strontium-90 (⁹⁰₃₈Sr) decays by beta emission to an isotope of yttrium (Y). Write the nuclide equation for this decay.

markingPoints.text: ⁹⁰₃₈Sr → ⁹⁰₃₉Y + ⁰₋₁e (or ⁰₋₁β)
nucleon number stays 90 and proton number increases to 39

parts.examinerComment: A common error was to decrease the proton number, as in alpha decay.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: The background count rate in a laboratory is {b} counts/minute. With a source present, a detector records {=k*2^n+b} counts/minute. The half-life of the source is {T} minutes. Calculate the count rate that the detector records {=n*T} minutes later, in counts/minute.

markingPoints.text: C1 for corrected count rate = {=k*2^n+b} − {b} = {=k*2^n} counts/minute
C1 for after {n} half-lives: {k} counts/minute
A1 for measured rate = {k} + {b} = {=k+b} counts/minute

parts.examinerComment: Most candidates forgot to subtract the background count before halving, or forgot to add it back at the end.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Explain why a source that emits alpha particles and has a long half-life is used in a smoke alarm.

markingPoints.text: alpha particles are strongly ionising, so they ionise the air and a small current flows
smoke absorbs the alpha particles, the current falls and the alarm sounds
alpha particles have a short range, so they do not escape from the alarm
a long half-life means the source lasts for many years

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers explained both the choice of alpha and the choice of a long half-life.

parts.label: (e)
parts.prompt: Describe how alpha, beta and gamma radiations are affected when they pass through a magnetic field at right angles to their motion.

markingPoints.text: alpha and beta are deflected in opposite directions (they have opposite charges)
beta is deflected more than alpha (much smaller mass)
gamma is not deflected (it has no charge)

parts.examinerComment: Many candidates gave the directions without explaining them.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: A satellite orbits the Earth at a radius of {r} × 10⁶ m. It takes {=round(2*pi*sqrt((r*1e6)^3/3.986e14)/3600,2)} hours to complete one orbit. Calculate its average orbital speed, in m/s.

markingPoints.text: C1 for T in seconds = {=round(2*pi*sqrt((r*1e6)^3/3.986e14)/3600,2)} × 3600
C1 for v = 2πr ÷ T

parts.examinerComment: Many candidates forgot to convert the period to seconds.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Describe how the speed of a planet changes as it moves around an elliptical orbit, and explain this in terms of energy.

markingPoints.text: it moves fastest when closest to the Sun and slowest when furthest away
moving closer, gravitational potential energy is transferred to kinetic energy
the total energy stays constant

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers used the idea of conservation of energy.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Describe the accretion model for the formation of the Solar System.

markingPoints.text: a cloud of gas and dust (nebula) collapsed under gravity
most of the material formed the Sun at the centre
the remaining material formed a rotating disc
particles collided and stuck together to form planets (rocky planets nearer the Sun, gas giants further out)

parts.examinerComment: Well answered by candidates who described the process in sequence.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Describe the life cycle of a star with a mass similar to that of the Sun, starting from a cloud of interstellar gas and dust.

markingPoints.text: the cloud collapses under gravity to form a protostar
it becomes a stable star when hydrogen nuclei fuse to form helium
when the hydrogen runs out it expands to form a red giant
the outer layers are lost as a planetary nebula and the core becomes a white dwarf

parts.examinerComment: Weaker answers included a supernova, which happens only for much more massive stars.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: A galaxy {d} × 10²⁴ m from the Earth is moving away at {=round(2.2*d,2)} × 10⁶ m/s. Calculate the Hubble constant, in s⁻¹.

markingPoints.text: C1 for H₀ = v ÷ d
A1 for {=round(round(2.2*d,2)/d,3)} × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹

parts.examinerComment: The answer can be typed as, for example, 2.2e-18.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: State what the cosmic microwave background radiation (CMBR) is, and explain why it supports the Big Bang theory.

markingPoints.text: microwave radiation of a specific frequency coming from all directions in space
it was produced shortly after the Universe began
as the Universe expanded, its wavelength increased into the microwave region
so it is evidence that the early Universe was very hot and dense

parts.examinerComment: Stronger answers explained why the radiation is now in the microwave region.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Explain why a stable star stays the same size for billions of years.

markingPoints.text: the inward force of gravity
is balanced by the outward pressure from the high temperature (energy released by fusion) in the core

parts.examinerComment: Well answered.

parts.label: (e)
parts.prompt: Describe how astronomers find (i) the speed at which a distant galaxy is moving away, (ii) the distance to the galaxy.

markingPoints.text: (i) from the redshift / change in wavelength of its light
(ii) from the brightness of a supernova in that galaxy

parts.examinerComment: Many candidates knew about redshift but not how the distance is found.
